author: Unknown
title: Marinëz
content:
Riceviamo e pubblichiamo questo contributo di

Elon Miloti

 che ci testimonia la lotta territoriale di Marinëz in Albania.


Nel paese dei miei, Marinëz (Albania), un’intensissima lotta autonoma ha ottenuto una vittoria enorme contro la multinazionale che gestisce i pozzi petroliferi del territorio. Marinëz si trova al centro del più grande giacimento su terraferma d’Europa e i pozzi, a decine e decine, sorgono su terreni di proprietà della gente del posto da generazioni. Regolati da contratti d’affitto irrisori rispetto ai profitti dell’azienda, da mesi non venivano nemmeno più pagati. L’auto-organizzazione degli abitanti, iniziata ad agosto, si è presentata inizialmente negli uffici in città. Per due volte li ha occupati. Presidio sotto il sole cocente, apertura dei cancelli a spinta, parapiglia con le guardie private, occupazione. Pur di imporre un confronto con i vertici dell’azienda, che si rifiutavano di incontrarli. Poi la protesta è passata direttamente tra i pozzi del paese, fino a occupare, la settimana scorsa, i locali amministrativi, rimasti occupati anche di notte, chiedendo un incontro risolutivo con il CEO.


La multinazionale cinese rifiutava di riconoscere gli abitanti come controparte, chiedendo di interloquire solo con le istituzioni locali e lo Stato. Ma se la terra appartiene a chi la vive, socialmente e legalmente, perché chiamare in causa lo Stato rimuovendo i diretti interessati? E soprattutto, perché farlo in un contesto in cui le istituzioni locali e nazionali sono piegate agli interessi del profitto? La domanda, ovviamente, è retorica e gli abitanti non si sono piegati: “Le trattative le facciamo noi”. Alla fine la dirigenza si è dovuta presentare, con il CEO in persona, garantendo lo sblocco immediato degli affitti arretrati e il rispetto dei contratti.


Una vittoria del tutto auto-organizzata: senza partiti, senza sindacati, senza deleghe, senza collettivi. Neanche per scelta, ma per necessità, visto che la transizione democratica post-comunismo è stata immediata e netta per privati e sfruttatori, ma di cancellazione totale verso organizzazioni democratiche e sociali.


Una vittoria gigantesca, ma che è solo il primo passo. Fin dall’inizio la vertenza ha assunto una dimensione politica profonda. Si chiede equità salariale e giustizia ecologica, ambiente e salute. I pozzi causano danni devastanti alla salute: patologie del sangue e delle vie respiratorie, accumulo di alterazioni genetiche e disturbi neurologici. In un contesto nazionale dove la sanità è privatizzata e cure e prevenzione sono negate. Per massimizzare i profitti, l’azienda ha provocato negli anni scosse sismiche artificiali o ci sono state esplosioni che hanno abbattuto le case, senza che molti abbiano mai visto un risarcimento. I lavoratori sono sfruttati e le tutele ambientali, già minime e insufficienti, vengono sistematicamente raggirate. Petrolio che scorre a fiumi, ma ricchezze ad altri, un paese senza nemmeno molte strade asfaltate e le esternalizzazioni negative, come le chiamano gli economisti, tutte sul groppone alla gente che in quei territori ci vive da sempre.


Quando arrivi a Marinëz, un paese di 5000 abitanti ormai decimato dall’emigrazione e dalla privazione, l’odore acre del greggio ti investe già ai confini del centro abitato. Dentro, si fonde con la vita contadina e coltivatrice, allevatrice e operaia: con i pascoli e le coltivazioni, i frutti e gli animali. Terreni da sempre della gente del posto, sotto controllo statale durante il comunismo -che in cambio, oltre a piena occupazione, favoriva attività aggregative e sociali, culturali e folkloristiche- che dal ’90 la popolazione ha lottato per mantenere propri, finendo però nella tenaglia della deregolamentazione incontrollata. Gli stessi vertici dell’attuale multinazionale cinese, nei mesi scorsi, sono stati arrestati per frode e corruzione, riciclaggio ed evasione.


Sono piccoli tasselli di lotte territoriali che oggi, mentre a Tirana la protesta nazionale va avanti da oltre 100 giorni, si interconnettono contro le prepotenze di partiti e multinazionali. Questa vittoria dimostra che, anche quando la coesione sociale viene forzatamente erosa, l’aggregazione ostacolata e la comunità privata di risorse e spazi culturali, la lotta continua a scorrere, quotidianamente, sottotraccia. E quando si organizza collettivamente, la società vince contro i prepotenti. Marinëz, aty ku nafta derdhej lume

author: Perseus
title: Πρώτη δημόσια επιστολή του συντρόφου Θύμιου Α., προφυλακισμένου για τη σκευωρία της Μαρφίν Vol 3
content:
Πρώτη δημόσια επιστολή του συντρόφου Θύμιου Α., προφυλακισμένου για τη σκευωρία της Μαρφίν Vol 3


1η ΔΗΜΟΣΙΑ ΕΠΙΣΤΟΛΗ ΤΟΥ ΣΥΝΤΡΟΦΟΥ ΘΥΜΙΟΥ Α.,


ΠΡΟΦΥΛΑΚΙΣΜΕΝΟΥ ΓΙΑ ΤΗΝ ΣΚΕΥΩΡΙΑ ΤΗΣ

MARFIN


vol

3


(…) όνοι παιδαγωγοί κι εθνοπατέρες,


κροκόδειλοι που κάνουν τους σωτήρες,


ο Ηγέτης, το τσακάλι, ο εργολάβος


του μέλλοντος, το ένστολο γουρούνι,


ο υιός ο εκλεκτός της Εκκλησίας


που πλένει μ’ αγιασμό τα μαύρα δόντια


κι ακούει μαθήματα αγγλικών κατ’ οίκον


ή και δημοκρατίας, αθέατοι τοίχοι


και σάπιες προσωπίδες που χωρίζουν


τον άνθρωπο απ’ τους άλλους τους ανθρώπους,


τον άνθρωπο απ’ τον ίδιο,


καταρρέουν (…)


Οκτάβιο Πας, Ηλιόπετρα


Προσπαθώ να σπάσω το μονοπώλιο της «αλήθειας» των ισχυρών, πλακωμένος κάτω από τόνους «λάσπης», πίστομα και έγκλειστος πια στον τσιμεντένιο τάφο, τη φυλακή, υπό την σκιά της δυστοπίας που τώρα ονομάζουνε «ζωή». Γιατί μια παρασκευιάτικη πρωία (10/7/26) έξω από το σπίτι μου και ενώ κατευθυνόμουν στη δουλειά, απήχθην από τους έμμισθους δολοφόνους χωρίς εξηγήσεις. Μου έτυχε ο κλήρος να κατηγορούμαι για το θλιβερό γεγονός στην

Marfin

 το 2010 που στοίχισε τη ζωή σε 3 συνανθρώπους μας. Μου έλαχε να συγκαταλέγομαι στην 3η κατά σειρά ομάδα κατηγορουμένων γι’ αυτό το θλιβερό γεγονός, που όπως έμαθα στη συνέχεια, στη «λίστα» αυτή βρίσκεται ο σύντροφος Κώστας αλλά και η συντρόφισσα Ελένη. Για 3η φορά, οι κάθε λογής δημαγωγοί και Κλουζώ χτίζουν καριερίτσα και με την ίδια αδιαμφισβήτητη σιγουριά, διαπομπεύουν εμάς και τους οικείους μας. Γι’ αυτούς δεν έχουν σημασία τα πρόσωπα αλλά η πολιτική εκμετάλλευση της υπόθεσης.


Και στοιχεία; Ποια στοιχεία; Χρειάζονται; Αρκούσε η περατζάδα του υπουργού δημοσίας τάξης, Χρυσοχοϊδη στα κανάλια και οι δηλώσεις περί «δεμένης υπόθεσης», η τροφοδοσία των «αδέκαστων» δημοσιογράφων με κατασκευασμένα «στοιχεία» και οι ανακριτές άρχισαν να εκτυπώνουν τα εντάλματα σύλληψης. Και αφού μας προ-δίκασαν στα τηλεδικεία τους, ήταν αρκετό ένα ανορθόγραφο ανώνυμο

mail

-τσαπατσουλιά που συντάχθηκε μέσα στο υπουργείο δημόσιας τάξης που στους δήθεν «δράστες» περιλαμβάνει και κάποιον που την εποχή εκείνη ήταν φυλακισμένος…


Ακόμα και σήμερα, την έλλειψη και της παραμικρής ένδειξης εναντίον μου προσπαθούν να την υποκαταστήσουν με την «σύνθεση του εγκληματικού προφίλ μου». Σκανάρουν

pixel

 το

pixel

 κάθε πτυχή της ζωής μου για να παράγουν «υποψίες» από καθημερινές συμπεριφορές, φωτογραφίες διακοπών και αναμνήσεις μου, καθημερινά ρούχα, μετακινήσεις και σχέσεις μου. Αυτή την φορά πρέπει να εξαπατήσουν την κοινή γνώμη ότι «έχουν ενόχους»…


Όλη μου τη ζωή δεν κρύβομαι. Αντίθετα, κατοικώ, εργάζομαι και αγωνίζομαι ανοιχτά και συλλογικά στην Αθήνα. Από που κι ως που κρίνομαι ύποπτος φυγής και τέλεσης ίδιων αδικημάτων; Τελικά ήταν αρκετά αυτά τα «αδιάσειστα στοιχεία» για να μας προφυλακίσουν. Αλλά ποιος νοιάζεται;


16 χρόνια μετά, δεν μου ζητήθηκε καν να δώσω εξηγήσεις, να καταθέσω. Με πετάξανε στην αθλιότητα των κρατητηρίων της ΓΑΔΑ, χωρίς καμία δυνατότητα να υπερασπιστώ τον εαυτό μου. 16 χρόνια μετά καλούμαι να αποδείξω ότι δεν είμαι ελέφαντας.


Ας τα πάρουμε, όμως, από την αρχή. 16 χρόνια πίσω, την 5η Μάη του 2010 ψηφίστηκε το 1ο μνημόνιο από τους νεοαποικιοποιημένους πολιτικούς-τεχνοκράτες-ειδικούς. Βάλθηκαν να σώσουν τα «σπασμένα» της κλίκας του Επστάιν και του χρέους των ΗΠΑ μετά το σκάσιμο της χρηματοπιστωτικής φούσκας του 2008. Μια γνωστή πρακτική αρπαγής, λεηλασίας και ιδιοποίησης που εφαρμόζεται από την στρατιωτική επιβολή της αστυνομίας και των φασιστών και την «κατά βούληση» δημαγωγία των ΜΜΕ. Με τα γνωστά αποτελέσματα: την κατάλυση κάθε συλλογικού δικαιώματος και κοινωνικής ελευθερίας, την φτωχοποίηση των μεσαίων και χαμηλών κοινωνικών στρωμάτων και την παράλληλη απότομη συσσώρευση πλούτου και εξουσίας στα χέρια ντόπιων και διεθνών αρπακτικών με γραβάτες.


Την ψήφιση του 1ου μνημονίου, όπως ήταν αναμενόμενο, διαδέχτηκε το κάλεσμα απεργίας που ανέλπιστα αποτέλεσε την μεγαλύτερη μεταπολιτευτική διαδήλωση. Πάνω από μισό εκατομμύριο πολίτες κατέκλυσαν τους δρόμους σ’ όλη τη χώρα. Ένα διαταξικό και διαπολιτικό πλήθος εξέφρασε με τη διάχυτη οργή του την αντίθεση στις κρατικές πολιτικές. Εκεί βρισκόταν και ο αναρχικός/αντιεξουσιαστικός χώρος με συνέπεια, σε συνέχεια ενός ψηφιδωτού αυτοοργανωμένων εγχειρημάτων που πολλαπλασιάζονταν ταχύτατα, ως αναπόσπαστο κομμάτι του συλλογικού αναχώματος στην επίθεση που δεχόμασταν.


Συνεπής στα καθήκοντά της ήταν και η πολιτική ελίτ όπως ο τότε βουλευτής, και νυν υπουργός δημόσιας τάξης, Μιχάλης Χρυσοχοϊδης. Αυτός που …

author: Michal Petros
title: Who gets to speak for Eritrea?
content:
Eritrea made its Miss World debut earlier this month, becoming one of the newest countries to join the competition since its founding in 1951. Miss Eritrea Snit Tewoldemedhin not only represented the country on this global platform for the first time — she won the

People’s Choice Award

. This achievement is a remarkable demonstration of Eritrean diaspora mobilization, but it’s not what stuck with me following the competition. In reality, the last beauty pageant I watched was probably

Miss Congeniality

, but as an Eritrean, it was impossible not to notice the paradox of Eritreans voting for the first time from a scattered diaspora, while those inside the country remain largely shut out of participation due to severe restrictions on internet access. It was equally impossible to overlook the irony of Miss Eritrea wearing a newspaper gown while representing a country with no freedom of the press.

Following 30 years of struggle, Africa’s longest war for independence, Eritrea officially gained sovereignty from neighboring Ethiopia in 1993. Since then, the country has remained a one-party state with no formal elections since independence and no free press since 2001. While the world’s attention was on the September 11 attacks in the US, Eritrea

shut down

 all independent newspapers and detained prominent dissenters, including journalists, politicians, and veteran liberation fighters. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) is presenting its

2026 International Press Freedom Award

 to

the Eritrea 16

, marking “the 25th anniversary of the silencing of independent Eritrean media and the arrest of some of the world’s longest-detained journalists.”

Though voices in the country are silenced, migration statistics speak louder than words. According to a 2025 report by the

Migration Policy Institute

, “one-third of the Eritrean-born population of about 6 million is estimated to live abroad,” citing indefinite mandatory military service, torture, and repressive humanitarian conditions as the cause for the growing exodus. Despite knowing the dangerous journey ahead, many Eritreans continue to flee across the border to neighboring Ethiopia or Sudan, and often onward toward horrific conditions in Libya, which has been the subject of many civil society protests in the European diaspora in recent weeks, including Justice for Eritreans’

September 12 protest in London

.

This isolation has taken on sharper stakes as tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea have escalated over Ethiopia’s ambitions for Red Sea access. Earlier this year,

AFP documented

 accounts on both sides producing AI-generated war footage — from Ethiopian tanks entering Eritrea’s port of Assab to Eritrean forces detaining Ethiopian leadership — images realistic enough that many viewers believed them genuine. Eritreans inside the country, with no internet access and no independent press, have no way to see this content, let alone respond to it.

In this vein, I’ve noticed a trend of tourists and diaspora visitors framing the lack of internet as refreshing, while subsequently sharing these narratives to their audiences for views and income. A newer member of the diaspora, 30-year-old Feven (pseudonym), spent the first 27 of her 30 years in Eritrea and believes the diaspora has a responsibility to speak accurately about the situation there. She shared, “Most of the good content I’ve come across comes from pro bono creators (

Eritrean Public Media (EriPM)

,

One Day Seyoum (ODS)

,

Radio Erena

, etc.). Although the people deserve to be fully or partially paid for their efforts, I can only envision grants as the way forward, in order to maintain a balance between the quality and the sustainability of the content.” Vanessa Tsehaye, executive director of ODS, shared that beyond limiting Eritreans’ interaction with the outside world, this isolation also denies the world exposure to the country’s multiplicity of perspectives. Vanessa is the niece of

Seyoum Tsehaye

, whom the organization is named after, who previously served as the head of the Eritrean state broadcaster Eri-TV, before imprisonment. Twenty-five years on and his whereabouts remain unknown.

Snit is clearly intelligent and accomplished, a neuroscientist, educator, and disability rights advocate. She’s also been highlighted as the “African Queen” by the country’s

Ministry of Information

, spoken at the annual Eritrean Festival in the US, and partnered with the Embassy of Eritrea to speak at …

author: Mada Masr
title: With region in turmoil Madbuly, Abdel Atty go to UNGA
content:
As diplomats and heads of states from around the world descend on New York this week to hold official and unofficial talks during the United Nations General Assembly, the already-long ledger of regional crises continues to grow.


In recent weeks the Houthis have taken key areas overlooking the crucial Bab al-Mandab Strait, triggering renewed fighting in Yemen. Meanwhile in Ethiopia, the long-simmering tensions in Tigray have boiled over, with the Tigray People’s Liberation Front

seizing

 on Wednesday the restive northern state’s three airports and setting the stage for what could become another complex regional war in the Horn of Africa.


This is in addition to the continued war in Sudan, the threat of escalation in Iran, the dire oil crisis that the continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz has created, and the stalled diplomatic process on Gaza.


Egypt finds itself at the intersection, if not directly involved in many of these crises. To represent Egypt’s position at the mega-diplomatic forum that is the UNGA, President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi called on Prime Minister Mostafa Madbuly for the second year in a row to lead Cairo’s delegation.


Sisi led Egypt’s delegations to the UNGA himself from 2014 to 2019. Since then, he has sent his foreign minister in his place: first Sameh Shoukry, who held the post from 2014 to 2024, and now Badr Abdel Atty.


The president’s decision to not personally lead the delegation this year, according to a government official, comes down to the fact that he “did not want to personally participate in the meeting of the Board of Peace, even though the primary issue on the agenda was Gaza — a pivotal matter for Egypt.”


“To this day, the board remains unable to take serious action to improve the situation for Palestinians on the ground — despite a full year having passed since the ceasefire agreement between Hamas and Israel, following two years of an Israeli war of extermination against Gaza — which is, of course, deeply embarrassing for Cairo,” the government official says.


The Board of Peace, chaired by United States President Donald Trump, was established earlier this year, with Bulgarian diplomat Nickolay Mladenov selected as the board’s envoy to the Gaza Strip. According to a member of the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza — a body established by the Board of Peace to succeed Hamas — the board is “completely powerless to even secure Israel’s consent for the committee to enter the Strip, or to allow the exit of 10,000 individuals selected for training in Egypt to serve as a Palestinian police force replacing Hamas’s police, even though Hamas has publicly declared its readiness to relinquish all its weapons.”


Although a source with direct insight into Egyptian-Israeli relations states that Cairo is maintaining all official and unofficial communication channels with Tel Aviv to address the situation in Gaza, this does not imply that the head of government will personally participate in Board of Peace meetings, given its limited effectiveness.


Instead it was Madbuly who led the delegation to the Board of Peace meetings to discuss the situation in Gaza on Wednesday.


Setting aside what a member of the team preparing for the Egyptian delegation’s visit to New York described to Mada Masr as Madbouly’s largely ceremonial role, much of Egypt’s political messaging is being handled by Foreign Minister Badr Abdel Atty, whose schedule has been packed with meetings. Egypt’s top diplomat arrived in New York on September 19 — two days before Madbouly — and is set to return to Cairo next week.


According to the team member, there are four key issues atop Abdel Atty’s agenda during his meetings in New York. The first is the situation in Sudan.


Egypt hopes to extend the UN Security Council resolution regarding the arms embargo in Darfur without expanding it to cover the entire country — a move the United States

pushed

 for earlier this month before the UNSC opted to maintain the status quo for one month.


Careful not to stir up a diplomatic confrontation with the US, Egypt is still trying to make the case that extending the embargo to all of Sudan would equate the “Sudanese national army” with the “Rapid Support Forces militia,” an Egyptian diplomat explains.


“Egypt’s stance here is not merely a reflection of its support for the Sudanese military led by Abdel Fattah al-Burhan. It stems from Egypt’s firm refusal to allow any party to undermine the national military …

author: Rosebell Kagumire
title: Who Does “Mutual Interest” Serve in an Unequal World? On EU Development Cooperation Pivot
content:
What is mutual interest in an unequal world? That’s what I was reflecting on this week in Brussels, when I joined the “Mutual interests in practice: How should Global Europe balance development, economic and geopolitical objectives?” panel at The Future of EU Development Cooperation, hosted by the European Centre for Development Policy Management (ECDPM) and Oxfam. The discussion came at a decisive moment, as the EU negotiates its next long-term budget and the Global Europe Instrument, while the Commission prepares for consultations with civil society and local authorities from 28 September to 1 October. Regional sessions include “Sub-Saharan Africa”, while global thematic sessions cover human development, the green and digital transition, democracy and human rights, and partnerships.

The EU is pivoting development cooperation towards its own economic, security and foreign policy goals through a “mutual interest” approach. But mutual interest means little unless it confronts the unequal systems that determine whose interests count, whose risks are ignored, and whose lives are rendered negotiable.

I spoke alongside H.E. Dr Naomi A. Ngwira, Ambassador of Malawi; Martin Seychell of DG INTPA; Christophe Lam of BusinessEurope; and William Roos of the EBRD, in a discussion moderated by San Bilal of ECDPM. I drew on the Afro-feminist work of the AfIP Collective, including members such as Memory Kachambwa of FEMNET, who also made a presentation, and the work of many African feminists challenging foreign policy in a time of faltering multilateralism.

For many in Africa, the EU’s pivot offers little that is new. Europe has repackaged its approach to Africa without altering the fundamentals that produce inequality. The Global Gateway has, by the EU’s own count, mobilised over €300 billion since 2021, including an Africa–Europe package of around €150 billion, and now targets €400 billion by 2027. But mutual interest is not mutual benefit: interests may overlap while benefits, risks and decision-making power remain profoundly unequal. As San Bilal writes in a new ECDPM briefing, wrapping every project “in a cosy mutual-benefit narrative is misleading.”

Africans have long critiqued, opposed and contested donor narratives and models of development financing and aid, calling for partnerships that are accountable and mindful of historical context. The pivot towards capital investment, with the private sector presented as the new magic formula, does not account for the reforms needed in relationships that remain hegemonic, rooted in a long history of colonialism and racial capitalism. Investment language alone forgoes critical responsibilities rooted in reparatory justice for the continent’s historic underdevelopment and exploitation.

The next Global Europe Instrument won’t escape imbalances. In its recommendations to the Irish Presidency, Oxfam warns that an explicit mandate to pursue EU interests “places excessive emphasis on the EU’s priorities over partner country objectives.” Development funding could build infrastructure for extracting critical raw materials, often for European firms and export, a trend “particularly visible on the African continent.” Fragile and conflict-affected states, which offer investors little, risk falling off the EU’s radar: left to their own devices, or pushed into extractive investment models that can deepen the very conflicts they need to escape.

Decolonial Afro-feminist perspectives argue that decisions and seemingly new approaches to trade, finance, security and cooperation are made within an existing unequal global order, its structures and relations, which distribute power, risk and harm unevenly. Who defines the bargain, whose trade-offs are treated as inevitable, and who is disposable before negotiations begin? In systems built to drain value from Africa, the same deal benefits Europe while Africa bears the costs. As economist Fadhel Kaboub warns, the colonial division of labour “locks you permanently at the bottom of the global value chain.”

Too often, “mutual interest” also means the interests of ruling elites: mineral agreements whose costs fall on neighbouring communities, and migration deals that serve regime survival. Amid the war in eastern DRC in 2024, the EU signed a raw materials agreement with Rwanda, which UN experts have found to back the M23 rebels. Several EU states are now in talks with Uganda and Rwanda to host “return hubs” for people deported from Europe. This is the …

author: Dr William Nii Ayitey Menson
title: A Child’s Fifth Birthday Should Not Depend on a Foreign Budget
content:
A fifth birthday should be unremarkable.


For too many African families, it is not.


An estimated

4.9 million children died before reaching the age of five in 2024

, and nearly six in ten of those deaths occurred in sub-Saharan Africa. Most were preventable with interventions we already know how to deliver. In Nigeria, the latest estimate is

116 deaths per 1,000 live births

, roughly one child in nine.


Judith Leveillee, UNICEF’s field chief in Nigeria, recently

told

The Independent

 that child survival will be one of two priorities in the agency’s next country programme. “These are the most basic of the basics,” she said. She also warned that short-term funding makes the slower work of strengthening systems harder.


The OECD projects that

health aid could fall by 29 to 46 percent between 2024 and 2026

, equivalent to $5 billion to $8 billion. Those cuts will hurt. But they also force a harder question:

how did we allow a budget decision made thousands of miles away to have this much power over whether our own children live or die?


Aid cuts are exposing weaknesses in African health systems. They did not create all of them.


I have seen this problem as a physician, hospital administrator, researcher, and now through health financing and policy. The amount of money available matters enormously. But so does what happens after it is allocated.


I encountered this directly while working on immunisation financing in Niger. Even when resources had been provided for planned activities, moving them through administrative levels could take time as approvals and signatures were completed. We began designing a mechanism to shorten that path and move some resources more directly to districts and facilities, including through digital transfers.


The work is ongoing, so I will leave the results for another day. But it changed how I think about health financing. Sometimes the question is not simply whether money has been made available, but whether it reaches the point of service quickly and predictably enough to be useful.


How money moves can matter almost as much as how much is pledged.


Years earlier, as a clinician in Ghana, I saw another part of the same problem. For people outside the National Health Insurance Scheme, almost everything could become an out-of-pocket payment. Even insured patients sometimes had to buy medicines privately because what they needed was unavailable at the facility.


At the bedside, the financing terminology mattered less than the consequence. A clinician could know what a patient needed, insurance could exist, and the medicine could be available somewhere in town, yet the family still had to find the cash before care could continue.


To the parent of a sick child, the distinction between an inadequate allocation, a delayed release and a stock-out is largely irrelevant. The child still does not get the care.


Ghana’s new Free Primary Healthcare programme is an interesting test. In an

analysis Banda Khalifa and I wrote for

The Meridian Letters

, we argued that it is best understood not as a replacement for NHIS, but as an attempt to make first contact with care earlier, easier and more reliable. It begins in 150 underserved districts and brings maternal and child health services, immunisation, screening and treatment for common conditions closer to where people live.


The difficult work starts after the announcement. Are medicines and staff available? Does screening lead to treatment and follow-up? Are resources reaching facilities and families paying less from their own pockets?


As we argued in

The Meridian Letters

, good reforms are not sustained by applause. They are sustained by design. Free primary care can make the front door of the health system easier to enter. It still has to lead somewhere.


That is also how I think about a

Fifth Birthday Guarantee

: less as a new programme than as a test of whether the financing system works.


No government can guarantee that every child will survive. But governments can identify the services most likely to keep children alive, cost them, budget for them, release the money, make sure the services reach children, and report honestly on what happened.


Cost it. Budget it. Release it. Deliver it. Report it.


The package will differ by country, but would typically include immunisation, maternal and newborn care, nutrition, malaria services where relevant, treatment for pneumonia and diarrhoea, and functioning primary care …

author: ROAPE
title: The price of becoming your own boss in Uganda’s boda boda industry
content:
It is said that Uganda’s vast motorcycle-taxi industry employs more men than any other sector outside agriculture. In Kampala alone, Uganda’s rapidly expanding capital city, estimates suggests there could be upwards of

300,000 moto-taxi

 (or

boda boda

) drivers currently in circulation out of a daytime population of roughly four million workers and residents. Moving people and things from A to B is big business here – and there is big business too in the alleviation of

boda

 driver hardships.


Fuelled by global venture capital and facilitated by both

digital technologies

 and

loose


regulatory

 oversight, over the past 15 years a new regime of

‘for-profit poverty reduction’

 has coursed its way through the highways and back alleys of this thriving sector. Through Buy Now, Pay Later credit products targeted specifically towards the

boda

 market, a growing fleet of specialist asset financing companies offer drivers the chance to escape a long-running informal rental system (known locally as

kibaluwa

) by one day acquiring a motorcycle of their own. Or to use the aspirational phrasing of one of Uganda’s largest moto-taxi financiers, Tugende, to

‘be their own boss’

.


The companies plying these ‘hire-purchase’ loans talk routinely of

‘win-win’

 solutions, bringing together their own profit motive with a mission to alleviate poverty in a way that feels compelling and seamless. Chief business officers in the US celebrate fintech in Africa as a

‘goldmine’

 where the ‘opportunity is massive’. One European founder has been described as

‘making better returns financing motorbike sales’ than he ‘ever did arbitraging gold and silver’

 as a commodities trader.


Beyond the boosterism


But how do these schemes work beyond the boosterism? In

a new paper

 I ask exactly this, drawing on interviews and semi-randomised surveys with hundreds of Kampala’s

boda boda

 drivers

between 2020 and 2022

 to explore what the process of becoming one’s own boss actually looks like.


The first thing worth noting is the scale of asset finance. Out of 370 surveyed drivers, just over half had accessed their bike using a hire-purchase loan and were either paying this down at the time of research or had fully completed one. The majority of these loans were with a specialist lending company like Tugende, Asaak or Watu, confirming

other


reports

 from Kampala that there has been a significant shift in this direction away from the traditional

kibaluwa

 model in recent years. As one driver explained: ‘It is now companies running the system’.


The next thing to note is that fully paid-up ownership can really deliver. Comparing drivers’ income and expenditure data,

the research shows

 that, on average, owners increase their net weekly earnings by a remarkable 73% relative to those who rent. Accounting for this is the dramatic fall in operating costs when regular access payments are no longer required. Essentially, ownership allows

boda

 drivers to retain more of what they make.


The long, rocky road to ownership


This is only one part of the picture, however. Though impressive, there is much that this overall figure conceals in terms of what the road to full ownership consists of. ‘3 Ps’ define this: protracted, precarious and pricey.


First, the journey to ownership is

protracted

. To make hire-purchase arrangements economically viable for themselves, many drivers agree to lower their weekly loan repayments by spreading out instalments over timeframes as long as two years. During this entire time, drivers spend significantly more per week on motorcycle access than they otherwise would – 36% more, on average, relative to those in the traditional rental system.


Boda bodas at sunset in Kampala (copyright William Kane Olwit, 2018)


To cover this, drivers must work harder throughout the duration of their repayment plan, leading many to talk of the ‘pressure’ that life under hire-purchase entails. In addition to the potential risks this poses from a

road


safety

 perspective, some riders also seek wider sources of support simply to help them meet their weekly targets and eventually pay down the loan, including through philanthropy platforms such as GiveDirectly.


Second, becoming an owner is

precarious

. Once included in the hire-purchase economy, drivers face a constant threat of loan default and asset repossession. This is underpinned by the basic tension that exists between fixed repayment demands on …

author: Paul Tiyambe Zeleza
title: The Historiographical Legacy of B.A. Ogot and His Generation
content:
Good evening, colleagues, and the Governor of Kisumu County, Professor Anyang Nyong’o! It is truly a pleasure for me to join you in this commemoration of the towering historian, scholar, and public intellectual, Bethwell Alan Ogot. I believe I speak on behalf of all of us in extending our deep gratitude to the Council for the Development of Social Science Research in Africa (CODESRIA) and the Department of History at Kenyatta University for organizing this important conference. Personally, my appreciation extends to that rarity of experiences, the opportunity to meet several of my former students at Kenyatta University between 1984 and 1989 who have become distinguished academics and administrators. It’s a befitting tribute to our intellectual father, grandfather, quickly becoming a great-grandfather, who was raised and spent his last years and is buried in nearby Yala, that this conference is being held in his home city of Kisumu, under the transformative leadership of one of Kenya’s leading scholars and public intellectuals, Governor Peter Anyang Nyong’o.


Introduction


Let me begin by noting that I last visited Kisumu in January 2019 to join Professor Ogot as he celebrated his 90th birthday. I first visited this city nearly forty years earlier, in 1980, when I was doing research for my doctoral dissertation on Kenyan economic and labor history, and spent time at this venue, the Tom Mboya Labor College. Professor Ogot had a lot to do with my interest in Kenyan history. My engagement with him goes back to 1976 when he served as external examiner at the University of Malawi.


Years later, he would proudly tell audiences at events where both of us were present that I owed my degree with distinction to him! In our classes on East African history, we had read Ogot’s books, and it was an indescribable honor and privilege to meet him in person. I was deeply touched and humbled when he asked to meet the student who had received the distinction, and he prevailed upon the department to bring me to the cottage along Lake Malawi, where the department took him to show their gratitude for bestowing the department with the distinction of his presence. .


That was the beginning of a lifelong mentoring and intellectual relationship that changed the trajectory of my personal and professional life, on which I will say more later.


When Professor Ogot passed away in January 2025, there was an avalanche of tributes in the popular and academic media celebrating his life and immense scholarly contributions. It is befitting that we are gathered here to remember and celebrate him as a towering historian and intellectual polymath.


Ogot belongs to an exceptional generation of the pioneering architects of the African academy in its multifaceted epistemic and institutional dimensions. These were extraordinary individuals, inspired by the fierce historical and humanistic urgency and imperatives of African nationalism: decolonization, nation-building, regional integration, development, and democracy. They were driven by the audacity, passion, and commitment to remaking the production, dissemination, and consumption of knowledge in, and for, Africa and the world.


They were scholar-activists who transformed existing disciplines and founded new ones, who built interdisciplinary and transdisciplinary paradigms, perspectives and practices, who believed in the power of education as a public good and engine of development, who relished their role as rigorous academics and public intellectuals, who jealously guarded academic freedom and the intelligentsia as the conscience of their new nation-states.


Their lives were large, complex, and multilayered. The trajectory of Ogot’s career is quite emblematic of his peers, born between the third and fourth decades of the twentieth century in the immediate aftermath of the formation of the colonial conquest state, whose ideologues deluded themselves would last for centuries, if not millennia, only to collapse spectacularly as Ogot and his peers matured into adulthood. I would like to explore, rather briefly given the limitations of time, five aspects of Professor Ogot’s remarkable life and legacy: Ogot the man, the historian, the institution builder, the public figure, and the mentor. Let me add that today we’ve heard much about many of these themes. My excuse for revisiting them is that I came a long way, and I have to justify my ticket!


Ogot the Man


Biographical reflections and commemorations …

author: WoMin
title: Women on the frontlines: Organise, Educate, Liberate, Celebrate!
content:
Across social justice movements, both in the Present and in the Past, education has been a central piece binding theory and praxis. It is from this understanding that, from the 17

th

 to the 18

th

 of September, the

Afro-International Feminist Organising School (AFRO-IFOS),

 a movement building space that uses popular education to strengthen our collective knowledge, share our experiences, and grow our international movement, hosted a School of Facilitators in Nairobi, Kenya, to support the deepening of a Decolonial Feminist Popular Education praxis across the more than 30 countries and territories represented, from Africa and the Americas.


There is power in naming the inequalities and wounds we carry as peoples who have been dispossessed of land, livelihoods, cultures and Knowledge. However, our greatest challenge is creating spaces that encourage us to dream of a world beyond the limits of colonial imagination.


Popular education has been a powerful practice for creating such spaces. Rooted in the knowledge and lived experiences of the people, it invites us to learn not only from books and institutions, but from one another.


Education is a political commitment


In the 1971 BBC film “

Behind the lines

”, Maria, a Mozambican guerrilla fighter explains that education was at the heart of why she decided to join the liberation struggle. In her experience

“If a girl reached a certain class [The colonialists] said that is enough for us, Africans.”


(Literacy Campaign, Guerrilla warfare in Angola, 1968. Photo: Augusta Conchiglia)


Our feminist

herstories

 across Africa and beyond have been deeply shaped by anti-colonial struggles. It was within the liberation movements that many women and men encountered education as a practice of freedom, in learning to question colonial power, reclaiming their histories and wisdom, fighting to protect their sovereignty and imagining forms of collective life beyond the impositions of heteropatriarchal, capitalist, colonial systems.


As feminist ancestor Nawal El Saadawi reminds us

“good education means creating dissatisfaction and disobedience.”

 Her wordsspeak to the transformative power of education to nurture the critical consciousness needed to both understand the conditions that constrain us and to connect them to our personal experiences, which is fundamental to organise collectively towards liberation.


But liberation cannot be achieved by a few, full liberation requires all of us. Our political project must be sustained by an intentional educational project that deepens our proposals and equips us to build the worlds we envision.


The educator is a pollinator


Through processes of learning, unlearning, relearning and imagining together, we become both teachers and students in our movements. This is one of the many ways in which decolonial feminist popular education inspires us to cultivate relational ways of working together that are grounded in mutual learning, listening, solidarity and care.


Instead of positioning the educator as the one who holds all the answers, popular educators create spaces where all can collectively formulate the questions that emerge from our struggles and where all can develop the knowledge needed to respond.


“Vou aprender a ler

 /

Para ensinar minhas camaradas

 /

I will learn how to read

 /

To teach my comrades”


Brazilian struggle song


The same way bees are essential for healthy environments, popular educators are an important part of feminist movements infrastructure. Popular educators nurture the power that already exists within movements.


Like the flower, each individual carries something that can nourish the collective. Learning is never only for ourselves. What we learn becomes a good we carry around our movements, to share, to exchange, to teach and to transform. Knowledge moves between us, allowing new ideas, possibilities and material actions to be activated. It is through this circulation of knowledge that we can produce the sweet taste of hope needed to build different futures.


Organising and liberating as we educate


“The beast is too big, and we need a political project that inspires us to build something every day and not just to fight and destroy the world as we know it.” –


Sandra, Guatemala


A decolonial feminist popular education praxis can build bridges across our different struggles, experiences, beliefs and movements, creating the conditions to move beyond simply resisting what exists …

author: Abahlali_3
title: March Against the Separation Wall in Cape Town
content:
4 September 2024 Abahlali baseMjondolo press statement

March Against the Separation Wall in Cape Town

Today thousands of people are marching in the street of Cape Town against the building of a separation wall that repeats the logic of apartheid spatial segregation.

The City of Cape Town continues to entrench neo-apartheid laws in post apartheid South Africa by building a wall that segregates and hides the poor from the rich along the N2.

author: Simon Ramapuputla
title: Cosatu congress adjourned after credential dispute exposes tensions
content:
The Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu) has adjourned its 15

th

 national congress after seven affiliates withheld their delegate credentials, preventing the federation from reaching the quorum required to proceed with the meeting.


The decision, announced after two days of difficult proceedings, brought the congress to a halt before delegates could debate the federation’s political report, organisational matters and resolutions affecting workers.


Speaking to

Elitsha

 outside the congress venue on Wednesday, Cosatu spokesperson Zanele Sabela said the decision by some affiliates not to submit their credentials was linked primarily to the suspension of Cosatu’s first deputy president, Mike Shingange, by his union, the National Education, Health and Allied Workers’ Union (Nehawu), shortly before the congress.


Sabela said the suspension had become a “bone of contention” because affiliates wanted clarity on why Shingange had been suspended on the eve of the congress and whether the move would prevent his candidacy for a leadership position. Nehawu’s general secretary clarified in the congress that the suspension was an internal union matter and did not mean Shingange could not stand for a Cosatu position. She said Shingange remained a shop steward and a member of an affiliated union.


The dispute was also taken to the Labour Court. Sabela said the court ruled on Tuesday night that the suspension did not stand, making the issue of his immediate suspension a moot point in relation to the congress.


Shingange himself told journalists that the reasons for his suspension were a matter between himself and his union. He also maintained that a person seeking a leadership position in Cosatu must meet the federation’s membership requirements.


Four Cosatu affiliates – Sadtu, Nehawu, Popcru and Sactwu – had organised a separate press conference outside of its mother body but it was later cancelled. Photo by Simon Ramapuputla


Cosatu denies clear divisions


The suspension and credential dispute unfolded alongside dissent among affiliates, with four unions calling a press briefing outside the Cosatu congress but cancelled it. Cosatu’s leadership played down the significance of the separate briefing, saying it should not be interpreted as evidence that the federation was fragmenting. They insisted disagreements among affiliates were not new and that similar tensions had been managed in previous congresses. Discussions among leaders during the two-day gathering, they argued, showed that the affiliates were not necessarily as far apart as the events at the congress suggested.


The precise reasons and positions that the four affiliates intended to advance at their separate media briefing were not fully addressed by Cosatu’s national office bearers during the federation’s own briefing. The issue was, however, part of the wider dispute about credentials, the suspension of Shingange and the conduct of the congress.


Cosatu’s leadership said seven unions attending the congress had not submitted their credential lists. Without those lists, the federation could not establish the number of eligible delegates for purposes of calculating a quorum. National office bearers said the congress spent roughly three hours dealing with the issue before the constitutional limit was reached. Under clause 3.4 of the federation’s constitution, the congress had to be adjourned and the president is required to reconvene it within 30 days.


So, the ultimate reason for the adjournment, was this technicality rather than a substantive political disagreement over the direction of the federation.


“We do not want to confirm what we cannot prove,” one of the leaders told journalists when asked whether political interests had influenced the events at the congress. The political questions that were supposed to dominate the congress included Cosatu’s relationship with the ANC and the SACP, particularly after the SACP’s decision to contest the upcoming local government elections independently.


The issue has implications for the tripartite alliance, which brings together the ANC, Cosatu and the SACP. Although the three organisations retain their decision-making processes, the ANC has long dominated its partners. During the briefing, Cosatu leaders stressed that the SACP was an independent organisation entitled to take its own decisions.


At the same time, Cosatu had been expected to debate the implications of the SACP’s electoral strategy …

author: Deogracious Kalima
title: Young Zimbabweans are being “kidnapped” and sent to rehab camps. Former detainees say they were tortured inside
content:
Former detainees say they were tortured inside.

Harare, Zimbabwe (Minority Africa) â

In the heart of Mbare Township, Harareâs poorest and most populated slum, there is a new and menacing economy emerging.

âItâs the drug trade and itâs on steroids,â says John Gwada, a community leader and pastor with the Zimbabwe Apostolic Church. Zimbabweâs youth substance abuse crisis has skyrocketed from 43% in 2017 to 57% in 2019, and is believed to be much worse today, according to the Zimbabwe Civil Liberties and Drugs Network, a monitoring agency.

This new dark-street economy is built on the broken lives of Zimbabweâs so-called âLost Generationââyoung adults born after 2000 who are the demographic most affected by the countryâs dire unemployment crisis. In 2023, researchers, citing social workers and addiction specialists, reported that 43% of school-going youths were hooked on illicit substances ranging from crystal meth (locally known as mutoriro) to tainted cough syrups and imported cocaine.

âItâs a mess, kids abandoning school, some chasing their parents out of their homes, others selling all the household furniture just to buy the next supply and feed their cravings for mutoriro,â Gwada says.

But the real horror isn't just found in the âstreet bases,â where the drugs are sold in small sachets and makeshift beer bottles. It lies behind the immaculate, steel-wire fences of so-called ârehab boot campsâ that claim to reform youths battling addictions, all for free.

Our investigation into Zimbabweâs mushrooming âdrug rehabilitationâ hubs shows that they have become a cesspool of corruption and brutality, where politically connected elites have turned a public health crisis into a money-spinning racket.

At centres such as Matrix Rehabilitation Centre, which began working around 2021/2022, and the Angel of Hope Foundation, established in Harare in 2018, former detainees and their families allege that the road to sobriety involves cash bribes, military-style torture, unlawful detention, and the disregard of basic human rights.

To a desperate parent such as Chipo Ganga*, watching her 17-year-old son waste away through mutoriro addiction, it didnât take much to fall for the sleek adverts on TikTok and Facebook promoting Zimbabweâs âdrug rehab colleges.â

âI was desperate to save my teenage son in 2025, the rehab adverts looked godsend,â she says.

The advertisements promise âholistic therapy,â âpsychological assessments,â and a path back to sanity, education, or employment for âsaved youths.â In Zimbabwe, where the formal healthcare system has all but collapsed and only 18 psychiatrists reportedly serve a population of 17 million, these seemingly non-profit rehabilitation centres pose as the only remaining hope for parents whose children are addicted to crystal meth, cocaine, illicit alcohol, or other narcotics.

The Matrix Rehabilitation Centre, owned by Tafadzwa Chidawa, a politically connected former police officer who was acquitted in March last year of an unrelated US $20,000 fraud case, and Angel of Hope, a foundation headed by Zimbabweâs First Lady, Auxillia Mnangagwa, are the most prominent of these so-called ârehab colleges.â

They claim to offer free or subsidised programmes lasting between one and three months to transform young people battling addiction into productive members of society.

But Matrixâs pitch extends beyond rehabilitation. In videos and advertisements reviewed by Minority Africa, the centre presents its programmes as a pathway to opportunities after participants leave, including education and travel abroad. Posts promote opportunities in countries including India and the United Arab Emirates, while others document participants obtaining visas and travelling overseas to study.

In one video posted in August 2026, Matrix celebrated a young woman receiving a visa to study abroad, before later chronicling her journey to India. The posts present such departures as evidence of what can follow the centreâs disciplinary programme.

Matrix has made varying claims about the success of its rehabilitation programme. In separate posts on social media, the centre has claimed success rates of 92% and 97%. The posts do not explain how Matrix defines âsuccess,â the period over which participants are followed, or what data the figures are based on.

author: Garhe Osiebe
title: The political economy of romance
content:
If there was any doubt that “billing” has become central to Nigerian conversations about dating, money, and gender, eLDee the Don’s return to music has supplied a new soundtrack.

On July 25, 2026, Olanrewaju Dabiri, better known as eLDee the Don, returned from a lengthy recording hiatus with

“I Wish You Well.”

The rapper, singer, producer, and record executive has long used popular music to comment on Nigerian social life. This time, his subject is not electoral politics or poor governance, but the expectation that a man who expresses romantic interest should also finance a woman’s needs, wants, and lifestyle.

eLDee occupies an important place in the history of Nigerian popular music. Through the Trybesmen and the broader Da Trybe movement, he helped shape Nigerian hip-hop in the late 1990s and 2000s. Songs including “Plenty Nonsense,” “I Go Yarn,” “Bosi Gbangba,” “Big Boy,” and “One Day” combined entertainment with sharp observations about social aspiration, politics, and everyday life.

“I Wish You Well” continues that tradition with humor. Assisted by comedian Lasisi Elenu, eLDee narrates an encounter with a woman he has barely met. She first asks for a loan, claiming that her car has been towed and that rent is due. The requests soon expand to travel, designer goods, and other markers of luxury consumption.

eLDee recognizes the script and declines the role assigned to him: “I ain’t the one. I wish you well.”

The joke is clear. But the song also opens a wider conversation about the changing relationship between romance, consumption, and gender in Nigeria.

In contemporary Nigerian slang, “billing” refers to requesting or expecting money, gifts, or material support from another person, often in a romantic context. Its meaning is broader than simply asking for help. It describes a mode of romantic negotiation in which attraction, access, consumption, and financial obligation become closely intertwined.

Social media has made these expectations more visible. On TikTok, X, Instagram, and Facebook, private relationship disputes are regularly converted into public debates: who paid for a date, who bought a phone, who funded a holiday, and what a woman may reasonably expect from a man seeking her attention.

The issue is not that women ask men for money, nor that material support within relationships is inherently wrong. Partners have always supported one another in different ways. The more consequential question is what happens when financial provision becomes the primary proof of romantic seriousness, masculine worth, or feminine desirability.

Afrobeats provides a valuable record of these shifting expectations. Nigerian popular music has long celebrated male wealth, generosity, and conspicuous spending. The ideal successful man is often imagined as someone who can spend freely: at clubs, in restaurants, on fashion, travel, cars, and romantic partners. Women, in turn, are frequently positioned as recipients, validators, or beneficiaries of this prosperity.

The arrangement may be pleasurable and consensual. But it can also turn romance into a marketplace, where intimacy is measured through transactions, and consumption becomes evidence of affection.

That bidding contest already has a name.

“For better, for OPay” is a useful play on marriage vows and Nigeria’s digital-payment culture. It captures a growing anxiety that romantic commitment is increasingly tested not only through affection, compatibility, or care, but through the ability to transfer money quickly and repeatedly.

This does not mean that requests for money are always manipulative, or that women from economically disadvantaged backgrounds are somehow naturally more transactional. Such explanations turn structural pressure into an assumed personal defect. Economic hardship does not produce a particular kind of woman.

But Nigeria’s difficult political economy does shape the practical stakes of romance. The World Bank has repeatedly identified poverty, unemployment, and weak access to productive work as major challenges in Nigeria. Rising living costs have also placed considerable pressure on households. Nigeria’s National Bureau of Statistics publishes regular inflation data that show the cost of food and basic goods remains a major public concern.

In these conditions, intimate relationships may become part of the informal systems through which people manage everyday life. Rent, transport, food, education, health care, and family obligations all …

author: Hassan Alnaser, Mohamed Alagra, Mashair Idris
title: Rizeigat clan bids for Hemedti’s ear, Burhan’s US visa troubles, Kordofan battles come to head as RSF presses ahead in Blue Nile, Kiir re-engineers electoral scene
content:
Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter


here

.


As world leaders gathered in New York this week for talks at the United Nations General Assembly, Transitional Sovereignty Council Chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan had to watch the proceeding from afar. And that is because, while the military leader had been penciled in to give a speech to the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday, the US denied his visa. 


For Sudanese officials familiar with the internal planning, the move doesn’t come as a complete surprise, given that the US had sanctioned Burhan last year and the relationship has become increasingly fractious. But the visa denial is yet another sign of the frustration and polarization that dominates talks over a humanitarian truce, ceasefire and political settlement to Sudan’s war. 


Sources in New York and others familiar with communications between Sudan, regional capitals and the US described efforts to mitigate the crisis, which they viewed as US pressure on Sudan to accept a 90-day humanitarian truce, while emphasizing that the government would not back down from its core position. 


But the military wasn’t the only one facing a political crisis this week. In Darfur, the Nawaiba, one of the Rizeigat’s main clans in East Darfur, announced it was withdrawing from the nazirate of Musa Madibo, the head of the Rizeigat. 


The Nawaib were keen to underline they still support the RSF leadership, who hail from the Rizeigat. According to a Rizeigat tribal leader informed of discussions within several of the tribe’s components, the move is really a bid to open a direct line of communication with RSF Commander Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo. 


Nonetheless, for the RSF, which has already seen internecine fighting among its base, with loyalists jockeying for rungs in the broader hierarchy, the move’s catalytic effect could create an even larger opening for rival military and political actors to exploit the crisis.


Away from political management, Sudan’s two main battlefronts continue to churn. Following weeks of military gains in North Kordofan, fighting is narrowing in on the remaining RSF-held positions. Both sides are upping the ante with front line deployments to try to sway the fight for the state one way or another. 


The military holds a much less firm position in the Blue Nile, even as it continues to prevent being overrun. With its eyes set on the state’s capital of Damazin, the RSF unsuccessfully attempted to take key towns that would have allowed it to create linkages in its supply chain between its positions on the southeastern border with Ethiopia and its forces farther south near South Sudan.


As wars engulf its neighbors, South Sudan seems set for its own breaking point. In a continuation of his efforts to marginalize his one-time enemy, one-time co-leader in power former Vice President Riek Machar, Kiir overhauled the country’s electoral process this week, appointing a new elections commission chair, amending the electoral law and dissolving the transitional government. 


An opposition source called the move politically biased, saying electoral rules set specific grounds for removing the chair, including proven bias, inability to perform the job or serious misconduct.


Elections are set to be held in December, and while voices in South Sudan and beyond continue to warn that current government practices are widening divides, Kiir continues to press ahead, pushing the country, perhaps, to be yet another blazing front in a region on fire. 


***


Rizeigat clan exits Madibo’s nazirate in bid for direct line to Hemedti, source says


Still from the Nawaiba clan’s video statement recorded in East Darfur’s Firdos locality, September 13. Photo: Abdelmged Abdelhmeed via Facebook.


After months of disagreements over leadership and representation within one of Darfur’s largest and most influential Arab tribes, the Nawaiba, one of the Rizeigat’s main clans in East Darfur, announced last week that it was withdrawing from the nazirate of Musa Madibo, the head of the Rizeigat. 


“We made numerous concessions throughout history under the nazirate administration, most recently under [Madibo],” Omar Nour, the head of the Nawaiba administration’s executive office, said in a video statement made on September 13 while surrounded by Nawaiba omdas. “However, these concessions were misinterpreted, and the reward was blatant and continuous injustice and inequality among the Rizeigat factions by the [Madibo] …

author: Jessica Corbett
title: Iran Pushes for A Negotiated End to War After Trump Rejects Ceasefire Proposal
content:
“There is no alternative to a negotiated solution,” an Iranian foreign minister said.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

As U.S. President Donald Trump publicly rejected Iran’s proposal for a ceasefire and reopening the Strait of Hormuz this weekend, the Iranian foreign minister reiterated that “there is no alternative to a negotiated solution.”

“There’s always hope for diplomacy,” though the Trump-led United States has been an untrustworthy negotiator, Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi said during a Sunday appearance on NBC News’ “Meet the Press.”

“We are fully prepared for the war to be resumed… We stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even [if] it comes to a doomsday war,” the foreign minister added. “At the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose.”

Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, explains why the US is untrustworthy: "In 2025 they offered negotiations, we accepted, then in the middle of negotiations they attacked us. Eight months later, again they offered negotiations, again we accepted, and again they… pic.twitter.com/dy4sfwOtgZ

Iran’s latest offer was “essentially the same bargain” as the June deal, “but with a very different sequence,” Sina Toossi, a senior fellow at the U.S.-based Center for International Policy, explained to CNN. Under the Iranian proposal, he said, “the U.S. takes concrete steps first, and only then does Iran ease its pressure over Hormuz.”

Araghchi and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had pushed for the proposal this week while visiting the United Nations General Assembly in New York City — where Pezeshkian said in his UNGA speech that “we have been the victims of terrorism” and highlighted the civilians killed since the United States and Israel began bombing Iran at the end of February.

Trump — who launched the illegal war despite his own intelligence agencies concluding that Iran wasn’t pursuing a nuclear weapon — used his UNGA address to threaten to “annihilate” Iran. Then, The Wall Street Journal reported late Friday that he “has rejected Iran’s proposal for a seven-day ceasefire and has told aides he expects to resume bombing Iran after the November midterms.”

The U.S. president on Saturday confirmed to journalists that “I’m rejecting their deal,” adding: “They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they’re losing so badly… We’re winning tremendously. We have total control of the Hormuz Strait… They want to make a deal, and I think that’s fine; I like making a deal, too. But that deal would not be acceptable.”

Despite Trump’s rejection, “U.S. official claimed ‘positive and constructive’ discussions are still ongoing between the U.S. and Iran through the mediators, including on nuclear issues,” Axios reported Saturday. Aided by Qatar, Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner “held a new round of indirect negotiations” with the Iranian foreign minister on the sidelines of the UNGA.

In a lengthy Persian statement shared on Telegram this weekend, Araghchi said that “we have seen the first reaction from the U.S. president, but nothing has been conveyed to us from the mediators yet. Of course, the U.S. president has also said many contradictory things, which unfortunately we hear a lot from him. We are waiting for the definitive opinions to be conveyed to us by the mediators, and we will make a decision based on that.”

“In any case, our conditions are clear; any progress toward the opening of the Strait of Hormuz is contingent upon the fulfillment of these conditions, and we will not shrink from them,” he continued. “Only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock.”

Such a solution must be “based on honor and justice that secures the rights of the Iranian people and fulfills their legitimate demands,” he argued. The diplomat added that “the people of Iran have demonstrated their strength across military, diplomatic, and economic spheres, as well as in confronting sanctions.”

Reporting on Araghchi’s remarks, Reuters noted:

The commander-in-chief of Iran’s army, Amir Hatam, said the war was at a critical and decisive stage, adding that Tehran would not accept a situation in which it was unable to trade while foreign powers used the region’s strategic waterways.

author: Dionne Phillips, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Indigenous New York Fashion Week brings family and futurity to the runway
content:
Details at Cheyenne LeGrande’s show at Indigenous NYFW on Sept. 11. Photo by Dionne Philips


Backstage at Indigenous New York Fashion Week (INYFW), Dusty LeGrande helped lace up garments from his sibling Cheyenne Rain LeGrande’s collection. A year earlier, Cheyenne had been there to model and help him with his own designs.


“It’s kind of so special because now he’s backstage with me, helping me lace up these garments, and it’s kind of nice that we can help each other out in that way,” she told IndigiNews.


The artist from Bigstone Cree Nation closed the Emerging Voices show on Sept. 11 with a collection that included laced-up mini skirts, tops with jingle dress cones and a wearable art piece made from 3,300 pop can tabs and ribbons.


A model showcasing LeGrande’s designs including the piece made from pop tabs and ribbons. Photo by Dionne Phillips


INYFW’s second year ran from Sept. 10 to 15, bringing together 30 Indigenous designers for six shows in Lenapehoking (Lenape homelands), on the island Mannahatta (Manhattan).


Just off Fashion Avenue, the American Indian Community House was transformed for the event, with seats lining the runway and fabric cascading to the floor.


Korina Emmerich (Puyallup descent) and Liana Shewey (Mvskoke), co-founders of Relative Arts and INYFW, organized the event with volunteers and professionals. 


The six shows featured Contemporary Culture, Emerging Voices, Knowledge Keepers, Thought Leaders, Luxury and Couture. Designers came from around the world, including several with ties to Indigenous communities in “Canada.”


A design for Creator Complex on the runway by Nishina Shapwaykeesic-Loft who is Kanien’kehá:ka from Tyendinaga Mohawk Territory. Photo by Dionne Phillips


Family ties behind the designs


Cheyenne Rain LeGrande ᑭᒥᐊᐧᐣ, brought their background in visual and performance art to the collection, describing fashion as “a way for me to tell stories and express my queer identity.”


Cheyenne Rain LeGrande at the 2026 INYFW. Photo by Dionne Phillips


Their work offered bright interpretations of traditional hide garments, including laced-up dresses and headpieces, with colour and fringe throughout. The collection also featured the latest version of their Moccasin Platform in black, which LeGrande said would be available soon.


“I think that Indigenous futurism is definitely a theme that is talked about in my work,” she said.


“I think it’s really special to see what emerging designers are doing, and what an honour to get to be a part of that group.”


Presenting a collection at INYFW was an evolution LeGrande said “makes sense” given their love of fashion and wearable art. Watching their brother’s designs evolve, they have also been thinking about how their own work might grow. They recalled conversations with Dusty, who has his own label, Mobilize Waskawewin, about what their work could become.


“I’m kind of thinking always about how do I take a concept, almost like a seed, and let it keep growing,” she said.


One of LeGrande’s designs on the runway. Photo by Dionne Phillips


Models walked to a song LeGrande wrote and their mother translated into Cree.


“She is a singer-songwriter who writes in our language and is a really big inspiration to me,” LeGrande said of their mother. 


LeGrande became tearful while describing a hug from their brother at the end of the show.


“I don’t know if I would be where I am in fashion if it wasn’t for him,” she said. 


“I feel so grateful to be a part of this and share my art with everyone in this kind of way.”


Cheyenne LeGrande blowing kisses to the crowd after her show. Photo by Dionne Phillips


LeGrande also had encouragement for younger generations hoping to share their work.


“You can do it,” she said.


“You just gotta create and believe in yourself and trust the ancestors; they’ll guide you.”


As the show came to a close, Emmerich commended the designers.


“Congratulations to the Emerging Voices designers,” she said.


“I’m so impressed by everyone’s work, and for a lot of them, it’s their first runway show.”


The joy of playing dress-up


Dusty presented his Mobilize Waskawewin collection in the Thought Leaders show on Sept. 12.


“My collection tonight was dreaming up what we’re going to be wearing in the next revolution, but that was truly inspired by my children,” he told IndigiNews.


He opened with a spoken-word performance.


Dusty performed spoken word to begin his runway show. Photo by Dionne Phillips …

content:
It’s time again for the weekly news quiz. What do you remember from this week’s headlines? Let’s go!


1.

 Udlu Hanson, Baffinland’s vice-president

of community and strategic development,

has been named to a prestigious list. What is it?


A.

 She has been named one of the top 10 most business-savvy northerners of 2026.


B.

 She’s one of Canada’s 104 most powerful women.


C.

 She’

s in the top 3 most impactful people in the world to hold that specific executive role.


2.

 Filmmaker Zacharias Kunuk has been honoured with a Governor General’s artistic achievement award. Twenty-five years ago he released

Atanarjuat: The Fast Runner

, which went on to be acclaimed as one of Canada’s best films of all time. What is he working on now?


A.

 A sequel to

Atanarjuat: The Fast Runner

called

 Atanarjuat 2: Running Faster

.


B.

 A documentary about Tallurutiup Imanga National Marine Conservation Area, and all the animals that thrive there.


C.

 An eight-part documentary series covering Inuit history, called

Qirngaqtuq — Fierce Prayer.


3.

 The Kivalliq Trade show ran Monday to Wednesday in Rankin Inlet. What was the theme?


A.

 Listen!


B.

 Big money!


C.

 You’re hired!


4.

 Speaking of trade shows, last week’s Nunavut Trade Show in Iqaluit ended with a gala celebrating the best and brightest of Baffin’s business community. Who won Business Person of the Year?


A.

 Kirt Ejesiak, owner of Sedna ROV Services


B.

 Glenn Cousins, of Kakivak Association


C.

 The late Rhoda Cunningham, who started Innirvik Support Services


5.

 Naujaat is celebrating a clean energy milestone with the completion of a $19-million solar project in the hamlet. Why did the

former Kivalliq Inuit Association director Helena Malliki push for solar panels in Naujaat?


A.

 Naujaat is located in a region that gets very little cloud cover.


B.

 Malliki is a self-described solar evangelist after installing panels on her own home.


C.

 Naujaat and Coral Harbour are not included in a proposal to connect several Kivalliq communities to the southern power grid through the Kivalliq Hydro-Fibre Link. So Malliki felt Naujaat needed an option to reduce the hamlet’s reliance on diesel.


Community leaders, government officials and project partners gather in Naujaat to mark the completion of a $19-million solar and battery-storage project that’s expected to supply about 30 per cent of the community’s annual electricity needs. Pictured here, from left to right, is Ernest Douglas, QEC president and CEO; Gwen Healey Akearok, minister responsible for QEC; Alex Guilbeault, QEC’s vice president of operations and engineering; Otito Atansi, QEC’s manager of alternative and renewable energy; Stephan Angotialuk, QEC’s assistant operator in Naujaat; and Jonathan Siusangnark, QEC’s plant superintendent in Naujaat. (Photo courtesy of Qulliq Energy Corp.)


Answers:


1.

 B — Udlu Hanson is

named among

 the Women’s Executive Network’s 104 most powerful women in Canada. She is the first Inuk from Nunavut to receive the honour since 2010. Hanson said she’s proud to be on the list. She also said there are so many strong Inuit women that she believes they should have their own list.


2.

 C — Zacharias Kunuk’s

current project

 is called

Qirngaqtuq — Fierce Prayer. 

It’s an eight-part documentary that starts with Inuit life pre-contact and covers the arrival of whalers and Anglican missionaries.


3.

 A — The

theme

 for the 2026 Kivalliq Trade Show was Naalagit, or Listen. It was broken out into three separate challenges to business leaders — listen to communities, to youth and to business.


4.

 A —

Business Person of the Year

 at this year’s Nunavut Trade Show was Kirt Ejesiak, owner of Sedna ROV Services. He recently received federal funding for underwater drones that generate images of the seabed around Nunavut.


5.

 C — Naujaat is

not included

 in a proposed project to connect five Kivalliq communities —

Arviat, Baker Lake, Chesterfield Inlet, Rankin Inlet and Whale Cove — to Manitoba’s power grid. “I was asking if we can get a windmill or a solar panel, and I fought for that,” Malliki said. “And it happened.”
