title: Πορεία για τα 11 χρόνια της κατάληψης στέγης Νοταρά 26, Παρασκευή 25/9, στις 20.00
content:
Αφίσες/Καλέσματα:


Συνέλευση Κατάληψης Στέγης Προσφύγων/Μεταναστών Νοταρά 26


ΠΟΡΕΙΑ ΓΕΙΤΟΝΙΑΣ ΓΙΑ ΤΑ 11 ΧΡΟΝΙΑ ΚΑΤΑΛΗΨΗΣ ΣΤΕΓΗΣ ΠΡΟΣΦΥΓΩΝ/ΜΕΤΑΝΑΣΤΩΝ ΝΟΤΑΡΑ 26 ΚΑΙ ΣΕ ΑΛΛΗΛΕΓΓΥΗ ΜΕ ΤΟΥΣ ΕΞΕΓΕΡΜΕΝΟΥΣ ΜΕΤΑΝΑΣΤΕΣ ΤΟΥ ΚΕΝΤΡΟΥ ΚΡΑΤΗΣΗΣ ΤΗΣ ΣΙΝΤΙΚΗΣ


Για τα 11 χρόνια της κατάληψης


Σε ένα κλίμα ανόδου του φασισμού και των αυταρχικών πολιτικών του κράτους και της δικαιοσύνης απέναντι στους ανθρώπους που αναζητούν άσυλο στην Ελλάδα, η Νοταρά 26 έχει εξελιχθεί από μια προσωρινή λύση στέγασης σε μια μακροχρόνια λύση επιβίωσης για οικογένειες και ανθρώπους που σε άλλη περίπτωση θα ήταν καταδικασμένοι στην αστεγία, στην απομόνωση και έκθετοι απέναντι στην συστημική βία του κράτους και των θεσμών του. Γι’αυτό τον λόγο, πέρα από το κομμάτι της στέγασης, η Νοταρά λειτουργεί όλο και πιο πολύ ως μια κοινότητα αλληλεγγύης, με δομές αλληλοβοήθειας -όπως η παιδική δομή και η δομή φαρμακείου της κατάληψης-, αυτοοργανωμένη από τα κάτω, με ανθρώπους που αντιμετωπίζουν τις επιπτώσεις του αποκλεισμού από τα συστήματα κοινωνικής πρόνοιας, τις νόμιμες εργασιακές συνθήκες και τις αξιοπρεπείς συνθήκες διαβίωσης.


Ακόμη κι αν φέτος δεν ύπηρξε άμεση απόπειρα εκκένωσης, κράτος και κεφάλαιο επιτέθηκαν με πολλαπλούς τρόπους. Στις 26 Δεκεμβρίου, η ΔΕΔΔΥΕ εκμεταλλευόμενη τις εργασίες που πραγματοποιούνταν λόγω ζημιών σε γειτονικά κτίρια, έκοψε ύπουλα το νερό της κατάληψης σε μια προσπάθεια να κάνει το κτίριο μη λειτουργικό και να το απομονώσει από τα υποκείμενά του. Αυτή η ύπουλη απόπειρα εκκένωσης δεν πέρασε χάρη στον αλληλέγγυο κόσμο της γειτονιάς και του αναρχικού χώρου που κατάφεραν να επανασυνδέσουν το ρεύμα. Έτσι, τα 70 άτομα που κατοικούν το κτίριο, εκ των οποίων σχεδόν τα μισά είναι παιδιά, μπόρεσαν και έμειναν σπίτι τους. Στον εντέκατο χρόνο της ύπαρξής της, η κατάληψη ήρθε αντιμέτωπη με πολλές περιπτώσεις που προκύπτουν από την όλο και αυξανόμενη ποινικοποίηση της προσφυγικής ταυτότητας μέσω των ρατσιστικών και αντιμεταναστευτικών νόμων του ελληνικού κράτους και της ΕΕ: γονείς που κινδύνευαν να χάσουν την επιμέλεια των παιδιών τους λόγω της στεγαστικής τους κατάστασης, γραφειοκρατικές διαδικασίες με εξωφρενικά κόστη, μέχρι και φυλακίσεις για υποτιθέμενες ενέργειες διακίνησης, εκ των οποίων καμία δεν ευσταθεί, και απλά λειτουργούν ως πρόσχημα για να φυλακίζονται και να εξαντλούνται φυσικά, ψυχικά & οικονομικά μετανάστ(ρι)ες.


Οι γυναίκες μετανάστριες είναι εκείνες που συχνά αντιμετωπίζουν τις μεγαλύτερες και πιο αφανείς δυσκολίες. Στις περισσότερες περιπτώσεις, είναι εκείνες που έχουν την επιμέλεια των παιδιών τους και καλούνται να καταβάλουν τα παράβολα, τα οποία συνεπάγονται εξαιρετικά υψηλό κόστος τόσο για τις ίδιες όσο και για τα παιδιά τους. Παράλληλα, αντιμετωπίζουν μεγαλύτερα εμπόδια στην πρόσβαση σε νόμιμη εργασία, καθώς και στη διαδικασία χορήγησης ασύλου. Συχνά, βρίσκονται αναγκασμένες να εργάζονται ατελείωτες ώρες σε θέσεις εργασίας τις οποίες ελάχιστοι άλλοι θα ήταν διατεθειμένοι να αναλάβουν: πίσω από κλειστές πόρτες, όπου καθαρίζουν και φροντίζουν ηλικιωμένους ανθρώπους· σε κουζίνες, όπου πλένουν αμέτρητα πιάτα και ποτήρια· ή σε ξενοδοχεία, όπου εργάζονται αδιάκοπα με μια σκούπα στο χέρι. Πρόκειται συχνά για ιδιαίτερα απαιτητικές και επισφαλείς συνθήκες εργασίας, με ελάχιστη εργασιακή προστασία και, σε πολλές περιπτώσεις, με πολύ χαμηλές απολαβές. Έτσι, μαζί με τις δράσεις αλληλεγγύης ακόμα και το ταμείο της συνέλευσης προσαρμόστηκε στις νέες συνθήκες και λειτούργησε πλέον σαν ένα μικρό ταμείο αλληλεγγύης, προς τις φυλακισμένες και τις γυναίκες αντιμέτωπες με τη ρατσιστική “δικαιοσύνη” και την ελληνική ρατσιστική γραφειοκρατία.


Το δίκιο το έχουν οι εξεγερμένοι


Στις 29 Αυγούστου, οι κρατούμενοι μετανάστες στο κέντρο κράτησης της Σιντικής Σερρών προχώρησαν σε μαζική κινητοποίηση, η οποία εξελίχθηκε σε σύγκρουση με τις αστυνομικές δυνάμεις και το προσωπικό φύλαξης. Κατά τη διάρκεια της κινητοποίησης, επιχείρησαν να προσπεράσουν την περίφραξη και να εγκαταλείψουν το camp. Πρόκειται για την έκτη εξέγερση που έχει σημειωθεί στη Σιντική από τον Νοέμβριο του 2025, ενώ μόλις μία εβδομάδα νωρίτερα, στις 22 Αυγούστου, είχε προηγηθεί η πέμπτη αντίστοιχη κινητοποίηση κρατούμενων στη συγκεκριμένη δομή. Μια δομή – στρατόπεδο, όπου οι έγκλειστοι μετανάστες έρχονται καθημερινά αντιμέτωποι με απάνθρωπες συνθήκες διαβίωσης, αντιμετώποι με τα ζητήματα που προκύπτουν από τον υπερπληθυσμό, τις καταρρέουσες υποδομές & την βία των αστυνομικών.

title: Dujuan Tayfunu, Japonya'da yıkıma yol açtı: 2 can kaybı, 2 milyon kişiye tahliye kararı
content:
Japonya'da Pasifik kıyılarına doğru ilerleyen Dujuan Tayfunu nedeniyle 2 kişi hayatını kaybetti.

AA'nın Kyodo ajansının haberine dayandırarak verdiği bilgiye göre, Japonya Meteoroloji Ajansından yapılan açıklamada, Dujuan Tayfunu'nun Japonya'nın orta ve doğusundaki Pasifik kıyılarına doğru ilerlediği kaydedildi. Tayfunun yol açabileceği şiddetli yağış ve toprak kaymalarına karşı başkent Tokyo'nun 100 kilometre güneyindeki Izu takımadasının en büyüğü Izu Oshima'da en yüksek seviyede alarm verildi.

Japonya genelindeki 5 günlük tatil dönemine denk gelen tayfun nedeniyle başkent Tokyo'da ulaşım hizmetlerinde aksamalar yaşanırken, bazı etkinlikler iptal edildi. Tayfunun, Tokyo'nun doğusundaki Çiba eyaletinden geçmesi bekleniyor.

Tayfun, Tokyo'da şiddetli yağmurlara ve Çiba ile Kanagawa eyaletlerinde heyelana neden oldu. Yetkililer, Çiba ve Kanagawa'da tayfun nedeniyle 2 kişinin hayatını kaybettiğini ifade etti.

All Nippon Airways ve Japan Airlines hava yolu şirketleri, Tokyo'daki Haneda Havalimanına giden ve buradan kalkan 270'den fazla uçuşun iptal edildiğini ve bu durumun yaklaşık 40 bin kişiyi etkilediğini açıkladı.

Nikkei gazetesinin haberine göre, Tokyo ve çevresindeki 6 eyalette toplam 1,9 milyon kişi tahliye edildi.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Steven Methven
title: How Zohran Mamdani Helped Germany’s Left Party Win in Berlin
content:
In Berlin’s state elections, Germany’s most leftwing party Die Linke has won a significant victory – the biggest in its

recent

 history. It could also mean that the city gets its first mayor from the party since the fall of the Berlin wall.


That’s partly due to the apparently infinite influence of New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose team helped supercharge the German left with the infectious positivity he’s world famous for. But it’s also down to policy – and in particular a long-standing pledge to expropriate housing from the private sector for public supply in a city where rents have

soared by 70%

 in the last decade. 


Die Linke’s Elif Eralp, a human rights advocate

sporting a ‘rent cap’ necklace

, may well become Berlin’s first anti-capitalist mayor since reunification. The daughter of Turkish immigrants, she led the party to a clear victory in Berlin’s Sunday election, taking 26% of the vote – several points over what the polls predicted, by running on a platform squarely targeted at Berliners’ cost of living. 


It all came with a little help from some friends. According to the Washington Post, in the weeks leading up to the race, Die Linke

sent a delegation to New York

 to meet with advisers to Mamdani. “The success of a democratic socialist in New York, the heartland of capitalism, is a huge achievement,” Eralp

said last week.

 “We’ve exchanged a lot of ideas.”


Die Linke, which has more than doubled its membership since 2024, was an early adopter of some of Mamdani’s techniques, not least of all

a massive ground game

 and

lashings of social media flare

 in last year’s federal election. In Berlin, they took another leaf from his policy rule book: keep it simple and keep it real.


Simple and real the campaign was, with a laser focus on

Berlin’s mounting housing crisis

.


Throw a stone in Europe, and you’ll hit a major city in a housing emergency. Crippling rents, gobbling Pac-Man-like one steadily increasing chunk of your paycheck after another, are increasingly the complaint not just of the under-30s, but many of those knocking up against midlife. And Berlin, a city where

84% of the population rent

, and more than half from private landlords, is no exception.


The monthly extortion that is the city’s rental market has been blamed for any number of social ills. Last year, Berlin’s

birth rate dropped

 by 5% on 2024. At the same time, some 160,000 people (a growing trend) are thought to have

left the city

, many for cheaper housing elsewhere. 10% of Berliners

live in housing poverty

. 


It’s a problem that’s been long-brewing. A 2021 referendum saw Berlin’s residents vote in favour of the city’s government

seizing privately-owned flats

 from large corporate landlords. While it wasn’t binding, what it proposed appeared legal, with Germany’s 1949 constitution – the Basic Law – giving the state the right to

bring private property into public ownership

 in exchange for appropriate compensation to former owners.  


Late last year, a

law drafted by political supporters

 inched the referendum towards a concrete reality. Enacting that law and forcibly buying back 220,000 flats from

multinationals like Vonovia

 at around 60% of market value was a major plank in Die Linke’s pitch. Another was rent caps. And that – no duh – seems to have worked. 


The result puts Die Linke far ahead of their nearest challenger, the centre-right Christian Democrats (CDU). That’s the party of Germany’s

beleaguered chancellor Friedrich Merz

. But in order to govern, it’ll

need to enter a three-way coalition

. 


Treachery aside, it’ll include the German Greens, who came fourth in this election also on a commitment to push the property law through. Die Linke will need the support of the centre-left too, in the form of the market-friendly Social Democrats (SPD), whose collapse in support has pushed them to a distant fifth. They previously ran the city in coalition with the CDU. Surprise, surprise, the party’s lead candidate in the city has already said

he’s against expropriation

. 


I predict Sturm und Drang ahead. 


Germany’s far-right party, Alternativ für Deutschland (AfD) also did better than expected in Berlin on 16% of the vote, with its leader bitterly claiming that

Die Linke wants to shoot the rich

. It also won –

though very narrowly

 – another state election on Sunday. In north-eastern Germany’s Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, it grew its voteshare by a stonking 21%. It …

author: Randi Beers
title: A case for rent control in Nunavut
content:
As temperatures drop and we start to prepare for another fall, we’re reminded of one of Nunavut’s most urgent problems: housing.


Andrew Morrison


We don’t need another study to make us aware of the crisis. We see it every day not only on the streets of Iqaluit, but in other, more hidden ways: students coming home with nowhere to live, families crammed into relatives’ homes and long-time Iqalummiut losing their staff housing when they retire. Too many people face various forms of homelessness in their own homeland.


The numbers back this up. The Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. reports that Iqaluit’s rental vacancy rate was just 0.3 per cent in 2025 — six empty units out of nearly 2,000. That leaves tenants with almost no alternatives and lets rents climb far beyond what many can afford.


Nunavut should freeze rents.


Rent control won’t solve the whole housing crisis. It won’t build the homes we badly need, and it won’t house everyone who is currently without shelter. But a rent freeze will help address staggering rental rates that seem to be going up every time we blink. 


Rent control won’t lower today’s already high rates, but it would limit how fast they can rise in future. Right now, Nunavut’s Residential Tenancies Act allows landlords to raise rent once every 12 months, with three months’ written notice — but sets no limit on the size of the increase.


For example, a landlord could raise rent on a one-bedroom apartment from $2,500 to $5,000 a month, as long as the notice requirements are met. There’s no cap. In a territory where buying a house seems more and more like a distant dream (or nightmare) and government staff housing regimes inflate the rental market, local tenants simply have nowhere else to go.


A freeze on rent can also have other positive impacts on tenant rights. Following New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s election on a rent-freeze platform, reports suggest New York landlords became more responsive to tenants’ repair requests, potentially reflecting the benefits of prioritizing tenants’ rights.


The path forward is clear. The minister of justice can amend the Residential Tenancies Act to let municipalities set their own rent-control rules, within territory-wide minimum standards. Iqaluit could adopt protections suited to its pressures, while Igloolik would remain free to choose its own approach.


We have a rental officer who hears landlord-tenant disputes. That office should be given authority to investigate unlawful rent increases, order repayment and enforce the rules.


Any new rules should cover all new rental units and should apply to housing paid for by governments and Inuit organizations. Rent control is also in the interest of the Nunavut government, Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. and other institutions facing steep staff-housing cost increases over the past 15 years.


Of all the housing problems we face, this one has a straightforward fix. The GN, NTI, and the City of Iqaluit should push for that authority — and use it.


Nunavummiut deserve stronger tenant rights and the security of knowing their homes will stay within reach.


Andrew Morrison is a lawyer and musician who lives in Iqaluit.


Nunatsiaq News invites readers to submit letters to the editor for publication. They must be less than 500 words and signed by the writer. Please send them to 

editors@nunatsiaq.com

.

author: Anneke Demanuele
title: Albo is proud to be a houso—will anyone else get the chance?
content:
“I’m proud to be a houso, and I’m proud of the community in which I grew up.” These were the words of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, spoken with a quivering top lip, after One Nation leader Pauline Hanson attacked his mother, Maryanne Albanese, for living most of her life in a public housing unit.

“Housing commission houses should not be there for people to live in them for 30, 40 [years]”, Hanson said. “And he said his mother lived in the same one she was born in for 65 years.”

Albanese may be proud to be a houso, but his party is ensuring that very few others will be able to access the level of housing security he and his mother did. Across the country, public housing is being eroded and depleted—homes and buildings left in disrepair, demolished or sold off to private developers. The idea that the government should build and provide long-term public housing to those who need it has been almost entirely destroyed.

In Victoria, public housing has been decimated. Walk-up estates have been bulldozed to make way for luxury developments, and 44 apartment towers are scheduled for demolition. The UN special rapporteur on adequate housing, Koldo Casla, has condemned the slated demolition of the 44 towers. In his letter to the Australian government, Casla writes:

“I am concerned that affected residents have primarily been treated as occupants of public property rather than as rights-holders entitled to participate in decisions fundamentally affecting their homes and communities.”

Demolishing housing will force residents out of homes meant to be permanent, out of their communities and away from vital services and infrastructure they depend on. All in the middle of a housing crisis.

According to the Victorian Housing Peaks Alliance, Victoria needs 377,000 more social housing dwellings by 2051 to accommodate everyone who needs low-cost housing. Instead of demolishing public housing and handing over public land to private developers, the government should refurbish existing stock and build new homes.

“It must be reasonably feared that the destruction of 44 public housing towers in central locations or the city will rather amplify these problems and not be a suitable measure to address these preexisting violations of the right to adequate housing”, Casla notes.

The Victorian Labor government says that the total number of dwellings will increase. But it will cut public housing unit numbers significantly. They will be replaced by a mix of community housing, run by not-for-profit agencies, and private dwellings sold at market rates. Tenants have fewer rights, face higher costs, enjoy less long-term housing security and are more easily evicted from community housing as compared to public housing. Data from the Australian Institute of Housing and Welfare in 2023, for instance, shows that when comparing public and community housing tenure length, the proportion of public housing residents that have lived in their homes for more than a decade is twice that of the community housing sector.

Residents in inner-city suburbs will and have been shunted off to outer suburbs, far from the schools, kindergartens and other services they rely on and that connect them with others. Many won’t be able to return to public housing at all.

This adds to the general erosion of the idea that housing is a human right that should be guaranteed to all. Instead of being an option for working-class people to live in, raise their families and build their communities over a lifetime, public housing is increasingly seen as a temporary option for only the most desperate—those living in extreme poverty and for whatever reason unable to participate in the labour market. Today, it is being deliberately run down to make its demolition or sell-off inevitable.

Public housing in Australia has always fallen below the standard of Britain and Western Europe. Writing in the

Marxist Left Review

, Jordan Humphreys details the limitations: “Access to public housing would be restricted to those on very low incomes, so it would be put aside only for the very poorest of the poor. If not enough of the poor could be found, then the Housing Commissions were encouraged to sell off ‘excess’ housing stock”. By the 1960s, two-thirds of British people lived in public housing, compared to only 4.2 percent of Australians (today it is about 2.6 percent).

The Victorian government’s housing strategy document describes public housing as a “legacy”, and what remains is intended …

author: Amira El-Fekki
title: Clashes flare around Warraq with tensions high as island residents campaign for housing guarantees
content:
Warraq Island residents clashed with security forces deployed intensively on and around the Nile island this week, with tensions flaring as authorities are yet to respond to the residents’ demands for clear answers and guarantees regarding the fate of their homes and lands.


The new chapter in talks between residents and authorities comes as families in Warraq take action to disrupt the government’s ongoing development project and seek firm guarantees that officials will support them to stay in their homes and lands.


Security forces set up on Tuesday metal mesh barriers at the entrance to the Qolaly ferry crossing that connects the island to the Nile bank, and, on Wednesday, more barriers were added in the vicinity of the crossing, according to a resident of the island who spoke to Mada Masr.


The measures, they said, add to a series of existing restrictions already imposed on the residents’ movement and access to key goods and services.


The new barriers appear intended to protect security personnel, after stones were thrown during clashes with residents near the ferry crossing in the preceding days, the resident said.


The latest of these took place at Qolaly on Sunday and Monday, with several residents injured as a result, including a young man whose skull was fractured in the clashes, they added.


To protest the security response to the Qolaly clashes, several residents also gathered at a demonstration on Monday evening near a security forces deployment stationed beneath the Tahya Misr Bridge that runs through the island.


The gathering ended in further

clashes

, according to two residents who were present. The confrontations were visible in footage posted by Warraq residents on social media.


As the ban on construction materials entering the island continues, the Qolaly ferry crossing, the main entry point to Warraq from Giza, has been a flashpoint of near-daily confrontations between residents and security forces for around nine years. One resident said to Mada Masr that the friction around the entry of materials to the island arises mainly between security forces and residents who work to deliver construction supplies to the island — but the clashes it triggers spill over to other residents in the area around the ferry.


The clashes come in parallel to a campaign to remain the island that residents have pursued since August. A large number of island residents have begun organizing as part of a group called Staying on Warraq, pushing for firm guarantees from authorities regarding the fate of their land and homes, according to several residents who have spoken to Mada Masr in recent weeks, particularly as circulating reports and unofficial maps of the government’s development project appear to include parts of the residents’ lands.


For years, residents have watched the development project unfold, waiting to learn what would happen to them, while their access to basic services on the island — like healthcare and education — has deteriorated due to state restrictions, leaving residents to establish replacements or alternatives themselves. Their efforts have included spending around LE400,000 to prepare schools for the current academic year.


They have now concluded that waiting has brought no solutions, as the state continues to carry out the project after

acquiring

most of the island’s land, the residents have said.


As part of this campaign, residents attempted on Sunday to obstruct the state’s road construction work on the island, blocking the way of transportation trucks involved in the state development project. The following day, they

held

a protest outside the New Warraq City Development Authority, where they vowed to escalate until their demands are met.


“People went out and stood outside the authority because the state is now building the roads, and they found out that the roads are getting close to residents’ homes. What impact will this have in terms of demolitions?” a lawyer from the island told Mada Masr.


“The state doesn’t solve anything. It wants to suffocate people so that they get fed up and leave,” one of the two residents who witnessed Monday’s clashes said. They said residents planned to continue disrupting the construction work being carried out by the state. “God willing, all the work will stop,” they said.

author: winter oak
title: The Love Activists
content:
This is the third in a selection of chapters from the book 

King of the Squatters

 by jaybo which we are delighted to be able to share on Winter Oak. The whole text can be found as a pdf

here

.


Here we are in 2015.


I do not recall my last night in Ireland, at all. I was extremely upset to leave Amy and all of our new friends behind. They got me very drunk to deal with the situation. When I arrived back in Liverpool, the Love Activists (LAs) had achieved support and notoriety in the city, after squatting six different high-profile places in a few months. The LAs had started out in London, declaring themselves to be anarchists driven, by love, to help house and feed the homeless and bring down the evil bankers and their corrupt system.


One LA known as ‘Grandad’ described the LAs eviction from the Bank of England to me. He said that they had been kept on lock-down, a prison term for everyone being locked up in their cells, for two long weeks by the police. The police had erected a tall steel fence which completely surrounded the bank and a cordon of cops then stood completely surrounding the fence all day and night. Upon witnessing this action local people spontaneously formed their own human chain surrounding the police and also maintained a 24/7 presence. Supporters cheekily threw many crucial supplies right over the polices heads to grateful activists who caught them on window balconies!


He said, “Almost everybody who entered the bank respected the building. Only a few made some graffiti on walls, and that could have easily been painted over. But the police did not respect the building cutting through those amazing doors.” Grandad also told me, with great pride, “The fire bobbies were called to the eviction. When they arrived, they talked and quickly decided that they were employed to save lives, not evict homeless people. They fucked off, to cheers from the crowd of hundreds surrounding the police. Ha Ha!”


Having been unceremoniously evicted from the Bank of England on Castle Street in the spring, the LAs had blazed a trail of six squats from the city centre, south, ending up on Sefton Park meadows. They had set up camp “right outside fat Joe’s new offices”, fat Joe being the name many of our people in the city used to describe the deeply unpopular

mayor of Liverpool

. The LAs had squatted a Georgian terraced block of houses in the city centre, and they did a sit-down protest on the road at the entrance to the Mersey car tunnel, closing the tunnel down completely. They had stormed the city, which had not seen any squatting in the previous twenty years, and received the support and admiration of thousands of ordinary people across the region.


As I approached the LAs camp on Sefton Meadows for the first time, it warmed my heart to see the anarchist flag that had hung from the Bank of England flying high, together with a Bob Marley flag. As I got closer, I saw a big banner at the side of the kitchen, next to the camp’s entrance, which read in large letters, ‘Uprising of the Homeless’. I never expected to read such an audacious banner and was utterly intrigued.


The LAs and Uprising of the Homeless (UOTH) camp was right on my old doorstep. Situated just across Princes Park to Sefton Park on the meadows beyond. A lovely, open site that had been left to the people of Liverpool, two hundred years previously, in perpetuity, i.e. forever, as a green haven in an industrial city. Sefton Park was one of Liverpool’s biggest and best parks, just a short walk from the city centre and the River Mersey. There were huge, magnificent, old trees surrounding the meadows, and about twenty-five raggle-taggle tents had been erected in the middle, surrounded by a rope border.


On a beautiful early summer’s afternoon, with everything I owned in my backpack, I slowly walked across the meadows towards the camp, full of anticipation. There was a group of mostly men sitting around a small fire. I saw Jed and Grandad first. They both gave me a huge smile as I got closer. Then I saw Lisa Love, looking like a futuristic steam punk. She also gave me a huge smile and had a very powerful energy. She seemed to have all of the men’s respect. Then I saw Biggy, and he gave me possibly the cheekiest smile I had ever seen. I knew immediately that I would be fine with the LAs and UOTH. I was definitely in the right place.


Most of the guys that I met at the camp considered themselves to be both LAs and UOTH. I asked about the Bank of …

title: Öğrenciler, öğretmenler, emekliler ve kadınlar Kadıköy’den seslendi: “Artık yeter”
content:
Türkiye İşçi Partisi (TİP), Emek Partisi (EMEP), Emekçi Hareket Partisi (EHP), Toplumsal Özgürlük Partisi (TÖP) ve Öğrenci Sendikası’nın çağrısıyla bir araya gelen öğrenciler, öğretmenler, emekliler ve kadınlar “Artık Yeter” demek için Kadıköy’de yürüyüş düzenledi. Süreyya Operası önünden başlayan yürüyüşte, “Kurtuluş yok tek başına, ya hep beraber ya hiçbirimiz”, “Saraya değil emekçiye bütçe”, “Emekliye kıyanlar milyarları çalanlar”, “İnsanca yaşamak istiyoruz”, “Bu böyle gitmez, gençlik biat etmez”, “Sermayeye değil eğitime bütçe”, “AKP’den hesabı gençlik soracak”, “Tarikatın bakanı Yusuf Tekin istifa” sloganları atıldı. Yürüyüşün ardından Kadıköy İskele Meydanı’nda açıklamalar yapıldı.

Konuşmaların ardından TİP, EMEP, EHP, TÖP ve Öğrenci Sendikası’nın ortak basın açıklaması okundu.

“Artık yeter” başlıklı açıklamada, “Bugün burada, memlekette her geçen gün büyüyen karanlığa karşı sesimizi yükseltmek için toplandık. Son günlerde yaşadıklarımızı yan yana koyduğumuzda karşımıza tek tek olaylardan ibaret olmayan bir tablo çıkıyor. Bir günde 6 kadın öldürülüyor. Manisa’da bir okula silahlı saldırı düzenleniyor. Geçinemeyen bir emekli, insanca yaşam talebiyle çıktığı eylemde ‘Para için değil onurumuz’ için diyerek intihar ediyor. Bütün bunlar bize aynı şeyi söylüyor: Bu ülkede kimse güvende değil” denildi.

Geçtiğimiz yıl da Maraş ve Urfa’da art arda okul saldırıları yaşandığının hatırlatıldığı açıklamada, “Daha okullar açılalı çok kısa bir süre olmuşken Manisa’da bir okulda silahlı saldırı gerçekleşti. Çocukların olması gereken yer okullar. Ancak çocuklar okullarında dahi güvende değil. Peki iktidarın çözümü ne? Okullara daha fazla polis sokmak. Öğretmenlerin kıyafetiyle uğraşmak. Çocukları ve gençleri hedef alan baskıyı artırmak. Oysa çocukların güvenliğini sağlamak; okullarımızı polis noktalarına çevirmekle değil, çocukların eğitim hakkını, yaşam hakkını ve geleceğini güvence altına almakla mümkündür” ifadeleri kullanıldı.

Çocukların bir yandan okul sıralarında olması gerekirken, MESEM’lerde güvencesiz ve denetimsiz çalışma koşullarına mahkûm edildiği vurgulanan açıklamada, “Makinelerin altında kalıyor, iş cinayetlerinde yaşamını yitiriyor. Milli Eğitim Bakanı Yusuf Tekin, MESEM’lerde iş güvenliğine önem verildiğini söylüyor. Oysa yalnızca geçtiğimiz yıl MESEM’lerde 17 çocuk çalışırken hayatını kaybetti. Çocukları korumayan bir düzenin, okullara polis sokarak güvenlik sağlaması mümkün değildir” denildi.

Geçtiğimiz günlerde yalnızca bir günde 6 kadının öldürüldüğüne dikkat çekilen açıklamada, “Kadınlar yıllardır kocaları, eski eşleri, erkek kardeşleri, patronları ve tanımadıkları erkekler tarafından öldürülüyor. Kadın cinayetleri münferit olaylar değil; kadınların yaşam hakkını güvence altına almayan, erkek şiddetini önlemeyen ve failleri caydırmayan bir düzenin sonucudur. İktidar 2025’i ‘Aile Yılı’ ilan etti. Ama kadınlar aile içinde öldürülüyor. İktidar ‘Ailem Güvende’ diyor. Ama kadınlar evlerinde, sokaklarda, iş yerlerinde güvende değil. Kadınların yaşamını korumayan; İstanbul Sözleşmesi’nden çekilen, 6284’ü tartışmaya açan, kadınların ekonomik bağımsızlığını güçlendirmek yerine onları aileye mahkum eden politikalarla kadınların güvende olması mümkün değildir. Biz sizin ‘Aile Yılı’nızın ne anlama geldiğini biliyoruz ve kadın düşmanı politikalarınızı reddediyoruz” şeklinde konuşuldu.

Daha iki gün önce emeklilerin Ankara’da insanca bir yaşam için eylemde olduğu anımsatılan açıklamada, “‘Para için değil, onurumuz için’ diyerek sokağa çıkan bir emekli, geçinemediği için intihar etti. Bir insanın yıllarca çalışıp emek verdikten sonra hayatının son döneminde temel ihtiyaçlarını karşılayamaması, açlık ve yoksulluk içinde yaşamaya mahkum edilmesi kabul edilemez. Emekliler geçinemiyor. İşçiler düşük ücretlere, uzun çalışma saatlerine ve güvencesizliğe mahkum ediliyor. Gençler geleceksiz bırakılıyor. Çocuklar okula aç gidiyor. Kadınlar şiddete mahkum ediliyor. Ve bütün bunlar olurken ülkeyi yönetenler sorumluluk almıyor. Bir çocuğun okulunda güvende olmamasıyla bir kadının evinde öldürülmesiyle bir emeklinin geçinememesinin sebebi bu düzendir. Biz bu düzeni kabul etmiyoruz. Çocukların okula korkmadan gidebildiği, kadınların öldürülme korkusuyla yaşamadığı, işçilerin iş cinayetlerinde yaşamını yitirmediği, emeklilerin açlık ve yoksulluk içinde yaşamaya mahkum edilmediği, herkesin insanca ve onurlu bir yaşam sürebildiği bir ülke istiyoruz. Artık yeter. Çocuklarımızın, kadınların, emekçilerin, emeklilerin yaşamını tehdit …

title: People in Diyadin demonstrate against gold mining: “Killing nature means killing life”
content:
Under the slogan “We Protect Our Land,” large numbers of people demonstrated in the district of Diyadin in Ağro province against gold mining using cyanide. The environmental rally was organized by the DEM Party and the Mesopotamia Ecology Movement. The demonstrators marched from the post office on İnönü Street to the central bus terminal. Chants included “Bê ax jiyan nabe” [There is no life without land] and “Kurdistan nabe goristan” [Kurdistan will not become a graveyard.] Banners and placards carried messages including “Kurdistan is not your mining zone,” “Killing nature means killing life,” and “Hands off my air, my water, my land, and my forests.”


Participants in the rally included DBP and DEM Party co-chairs Çiğdem Kılıçgün Uçar and Tuncer Bakırhan, as well as representatives of various environmental groups. The protest was directed against a gold mining project near the village of Mollakara. Environmental organizations and municipalities in the region have warned in particular about the potential impact of cyanide use on the Murat River and its watershed.


‘We are fighting for every place that is being plundered’


Alev Yılmaz of the Varto Ecology Platform recalled the resistance against energy and resource extraction projects in Varto, which has been ongoing for more than 140 days. She stressed that the protest there was not limited to their own region: “We are waging this resistance not only for Varto, but for every place that is being plundered.”


Rojhat Özgökçe of the Mesopotamia Ecology Movement spoke of the long-standing exploitation of Kurdistan’s natural environment. At the same time, he said, the experiences in Varto and Karlıova showed that an organized ecological movement was emerging in response. “We must become stronger, organize ourselves, and develop a powerful struggle against ecocide,” Özgökçe said.


Uçar: Land is more valuable than gold


DBP (Democratic Regions Party) co-chair Çiğdem Kılıçgün Uçar linked the mining projects to poverty, migration, and the economic exploitation of the region. “Why have the people of Diyadin migrated away? Because deep poverty was left behind here,” Uçar said. She noted that attempts were now being made to bring companies into the region and exploit Diyadin. “What we must do, therefore, is protect our land. The land and the resistance of the people of Diyadin are more valuable than gold.”


She rejected claims that mining companies would bring jobs to the region: “Our people are being offered toxic employment. No one accepts the plundering of their air, water, and livelihoods. We will not accept it either.”


Uçar said that exploitation was taking place from Muş and Diyarbakır to Ağrı without regard for the people living there. “We also want to leave a dignified life for the seven-year-old children standing here in this square today.”


Uçar also called on local residents not to sell their land to mining companies: “They are trying to buy up land in the villages piece by piece. Do not sell your land.”


Ecology and peace


Referring to Abdullah Öcalan’s call of February 27, 2025, Uçar linked the protection of natural resources and ecosystems to the peace and democratic society process. “Those who do not protect their nature do not protect peace either,” the politician said. “We must begin by protecting the water and nature of this land, especially Kurdistan.” She said that companies were poised to exploit the region’s natural and social resources. “We will stand against them together in this struggle.”


Bakırhan: Kurdish population faces renewed displacement


DEM Party (Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party) co-chair Tuncer Bakırhan drew a connection between today’s mining projects and the displacement of the Kurdish population in previous decades. He recalled that millions of Kurds were forced to leave their villages, pastures, mountains, and homes as a result of war and violence in the 1990s. “Now they are trying to displace the Kurdish population for a second time through mining companies and profiteers,” Bakırhan said.


The resistance, he said, was not limited to Diyadin. “From Lice to Varto and Karlıova, and from the Ida Mountains to Akbelen Forest, people are resisting environmental destruction and profit-driven interests. We say: Do not blast our mountains, do not pollute our plains, do not pollute our water. The people will not surrender their land to companies that want to poison it, extract a little gold, and then disappear.”

author: groundxero
title: ‘Bit of an overkill’: 123 detained after Jantar Mantar protest for Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation including journalist and minor
content:
Hours after the Cockroach Janta Party’s ultimatum to the BJP run incumbent Union government to resume the massive mass protests that shook the capital in late July earlier this year if the Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar does not tender his resignation within two days, Jantar Mantar has been put on lockdown. At least 123 protesters were detained and taken to various police stations in the outskirts of the city. 


 


by

Mouli Sharma


 


25 September 2026, New Delhi:

 “There were more policemen than protesters in sight,” says Nandita Narain, who arrived on site at around 2:10 PM. One of the panelists invited to speak at the demonstration, she was unable to even enter the protest venue, being trapped within an onslaught of khaki clad policemen and Rapid Action Forces. 


 


“Some of them looked as old as the hills, you know,” she says. Narain is a retired professor of Mathematics from the University of Delhi, and a veteran of Delhi’s activist frontline, so she knows a thing or two about experience. “These are clearly people who’ve just been given uniforms and I don’t know… some of them were looking really way beyond the retirement age,” she says.


 


“But then one can’t be sure,” she’s quick to add.


 


The protest at Jantar Mantar on Friday afternoon was called for on an urgent basis by the Cockroach Janta Party leadership–namely Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das, Ratna Singh, and others of the anti-paper leak movement’s fame from June-August 2026, which brought tens of thousands of people onto the streets in cities across India, and succeeded in pressurising a Union Minister to resign following gross governance failures for the first time since the BJP-led NDA alliance came to power in 2014. This time, though, the focus has moved from education to elections—the second item on the CJP’s manifesto since the satirical outfit was ‘established’ earlier this year. 


 


“If any legit vote is deleted, whether in a CJP or opposition-ruled state, the CEC shall be arrested under UAPA, as taking away voting rights of citizens is no less than terrorism,” the second item of the five point manifesto reads (next up are women’s parliamentary reservation, audits of Godi media finances, and a 20 year ban on defectors (the first item, which opposes retirement rewards for Chief Justices, may also return to the roster)). As such, the ‘

school thik karo abhiyan

’ which say ground level campaigning by CJP volunteers in urban and rural government schools and exposed failures of governance and misappropriation of funds at the grassroots level in public education, has taken a backseat, as the ruling party’s Special Intensive Revision has placed the very essence of India’s democratic identity at peril. 


 


The CJP has put forth three demands: First being ‘immediate accountability’. 


 


“We demand the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar in 48 hours,” the outfit says. They also demand the initiation of criminal proceedings and answer to the question, “Who gave him the orders?”


 


The second demand is an immediate terminus on elections and SIR. “Put all upcoming polls on hold,” the party says, addressing the government. “Freeze SIR and roll back to the January 2025 voter list. Constitute an Independent Inquiry Commission to examine how SIR decisions were taken. Direct the Supreme Court to seize all files related to SIR and its decision-making process.”


 


The third demand is that of an ‘independent leadership’: “Repeal the 2023 law on the appointment of Election Commissioners,” they say. “Enact a new law that inspires public confidence, with active participation from civil society.”


 


The structure is identical to that of the movement against paper leaks and corruption in the Higher Education Sector that became the start of CJP’s transition from screen to street on June 6 2026, when CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke’s flight first landed in India at the start of what would become one of the most significant nationwide mass agitations in recent history. But the state’s response is far from comparable.


 


“There were such few people, and such a huge number of cops,” said a protester outside Jantar Mantar, who had narrowly escaped detention. “If they just allowed it to happen, then what would have been the big deal? It’s not as if it was a huge crowd.”

author: David Palumbo-Liu
title: Pro-Palestine Stanford Students Celebrate Dismissal of Harsh Charges
content:
All charges were dropped against the students, who could have faced prison for “conspiracy to trespass” and vandalism.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

This week a judge dismissed all the charges brought against a group of Stanford students for occupying the university president’s office in June 2024 to protest Stanford’s complicity in Israel’s genocide in Gaza. The judge also reduced the amount of restitution to roughly $52,000 total, which ended up being paid by an anonymous source.

The September 21 decision came down despite the strenuous efforts of Stanford University and the Office of the District Attorney of Santa Clara County, California.

The charges against the Stanford protesters were the most severe of any imposed on pro-Palestine student activists in the United States. Their dismissal is a cause for celebration, but it also gives us an opportunity to better understand how universities attempt to suppress activism for Palestine.

The students took over the office of Stanford University President Richard Saller after the university refused to act according to its own standards for ethical investments — it was not a sudden, impetuous act.

There were three different protests for Palestine at Stanford that took place between October 2023 and June 2024. Shortly after October 7, 2023, a group of students took over White Plaza, an outdoor campus space designated as a free speech zone. When I visited at the start of the protest, they had set up three large tents and some tables, and dug in. They called the encampment the Sit-In to Stop Genocide, and they used the space they had claimed to hold public events, speeches, and rallies. They stayed there 24/7, even over the winter break. As the encampment grew exponentially, students created communications networks and mutual support with the greater Palo Alto community.

At one point, university administrators told participants in the sit-in to bring the action to an end, but within four hours, a huge crowd of community members formed a circle around the encampment to defend it. Students sat on pieces of cardboard to do assignments on their laptops, shared food, and danced overnight. When university administrators indicated that they would begin talks with the student activists, the sit-in ended. The university removed the tents and all materials in February 2024.

A report by the Stanford Muslim, Arab, and Palestinian Communities Committee recounts how, months later, in April 2024, dismayed by the lack of progress in the negotiations, “a group of pro-Palestinian students organized a rally that then resulted in a second sit-in known as the People’s University for Palestine.”

The rally drew a huge crowd that marched through the campus.

Afterward, protesters turned the grassy space into “People’s University” — an encampment that held classes, hosted speakers, showed films, and organized morning breakfasts and evening prayers.

When talks with the university completely broke down in late May, a group (including those who are now known as the “Stanford 11”) took over the university president’s office. This occupation was short-lived: Within hours, the police had broken into the building and hauled the protesters to jail.

This is when Stanford, one of the wealthiest universities in the world, went into high gear. It tore down the encampment and started disciplinary proceedings. Stanford went so far as to initially push for the prosecution of a Stanford Daily reporter who was in the building to report on the event. As the Columbia Journalism Review noted, “Even as the case languished for months, Stanford wanted prosecutors to pursue it.”

Disciplinary hearings began. Students lost housing and were removed from campus. Eventually, District Attorney Jeff Rosen charged them with felonies and conspiracy. At their trial, which I attended, the district attorney’s office repeatedly claimed that the Stanford 11 had “f***ed it up” for the peaceful protesters, who were civilly obedient.

Before and during the protests, Stanford students had followed the required steps and passed divestment resolutions asking that Stanford follow its own policy on investments, which states:

The Trustees recognize that many issues of broad social and political concern raised by members of the University community are worthy of debate and study. Consistent with the University’s …

Pese a estar señalizado como Sitio de Memoria, el lugar se encuentra afectado al uso de la Policía Bonaerense y nunca se han abierto sus archivos.

author: Joe Sandler Clarke
title: Weapons Firm Gave Advice to UK Universities on Countering Gaza Protests
content:
British weapons manufacturer BAE Systems worked with UK universities to counter campus protests against Israel’s genocide in Gaza, according to emails and internal documents. 


An investigation by

Liberty Investigates and Al Jazeera

 found 13 UK universities spoke with the firm about how to handle demonstrations. 


In 2024, the company appeared to have urged universities “to counteract an often skewed, but prominent narrative from protesters” about its partnership with higher education institutions,

slides from a presentation

 show. 


Staff members from one top institution spoke with BAE before disciplining student activists. Another interacted with the company about an upcoming protest against the firm. 


BAE Systems supplies Israel with parts for

F-35 fighter jets

, which have played a

key role

 in the Israeli military’s destruction of Gaza.


The 13 universities identified – including Manchester University, Nottingham University, Sheffield University, Southampton University, Birmingham University, Strathclyde and Cranfield – collectively receive as much as £15m via agreements for research funding with the arms manufacturer, according to the investigation. 


Meanwhile, BAE has active “

strategic partnerships

” with Manchester, Strathclyde, Cranfield, Nottingham and Southampton to work on research projects in areas like “AI, quantum mechanics, manufacturing, cyber and aerospace”. 


At Sheffield University, students protested an October 2024 online careers event featuring BAE. A university staff member then spoke with BAE before disciplining four people, according to the documents, which were obtained using freedom of information rules. 


The university insisted disciplinary procedures “are independent and not influenced by any external partnerships” and that it “consults all parties involved to ensure a fair process”.


In November 2025, a Southampton University staff member passed news of a planned protest to BAE. The university denied it had worked with BAE to come up with a counter-narrative to protesters’ criticisms of its links to the firm. 


Gina Romero, the UN special rapporteur for peaceful assembly and association, told Al Jazeera the findings represented a “troubling pattern” of institutions taking “operational cues and security strategies from weapons manufacturers to suppress their own students”.


In July, the

UK government announced a new partnership

 between arms firms, including BAE, and several universities to support “vital research into new defence technologies”.


Several universities have clamped down hard on student activists over their support for Palestine. King’s College London, not named in this story,

disciplined 26 students

 for pro-Palestine activism between October 2023 and November 2025, more than any UK institution. Egyptian student Usama Ghanem temporarily had his visa sponsorship withdrawn by the university,

threatening his ability to remain in the UK

author: Davao Today
title: Students rally on Martial Law commemoration despite arrest threats
content:
“We should show that we are strong, that we are united here.”

On the 54th year of Martial Law imposition, students joined nationwide protests calling for remembrance, accountability and action.

They took to the streets despite heightened police presence and recent arrests of protesters.

For some students who joined the 54th anniversary commemoration of Martial Law on September 21, the possibility of arrest was not enough to keep them away from the streets. Instead, they said the risks reinforced the importance of being present.

For Alyssa (surname withheld), a Visual Communication student from the University of the Philippines Diliman College of Fine Arts, joining the commemoration was rooted in the right to speak and remember the victims of the dictatorship. “I think the reason why we are here is because even if there are activists being arrested, we should not be afraid to express our call because it is our right to speak.”

She said that the commemoration should not be reduced to a historical date, pointing to the victims of Martial Law and continuing concerns over the treatment of activists.

The National Capital Region Police Office placed Metro Manila on full alert, with more than 15,700 personnel deployed for the September 21 activities. Police said that the deployment was intended to maintain public safety while allowing peaceful assemblies.

The heightened security also followed clashes during the previous year’s September 21 demonstrations when police reported arrests and injuries after violence broke out in parts of Manila.

For Jake Bitar, a Grade 12 student of City of Mandaluyong High School, the presence of police and reports of arrests did not change his decision to attend. “We are here to show that we are together, that we will not forget,” Bitar said. “I think it’s very important because we are here to study what is really happening. We are here to show that we are not afraid.”

He urged fellow students to remain united despite threats. “Even if we are being threatened or there are many threats, we should be here. We should show that we are strong, that we are united here.”

This year’s commemoration also became a venue for protests against corruption and demands for government accountability. Kabataan Party-list Rep. Renee Co highlighted the opportunity to connect the historical legacy of Martial Law with present-day concerns over corruption and accountability. “We remember the widespread human rights violations and corruption that occurred then and continue to this day.”

Co also called for accountability and justice, stressing that the Marcoses have not yet been held accountable and that their ill-gotten wealth has not been fully recovered.

She criticized the heavy police presence surrounding the protests. She said that authorities were prepared to manage demonstrations but were less responsive when it came to demands for accountability from those accused of corruption.

She said that the protesters’ calls would continue despite police barriers and other security measures. “The ranks of police, rows of barbed wire and concrete barriers, or even tear gas and batons cannot stop the anger of thousands of young people who are being robbed of their future.”

For Alyssa, participating in mobilizations is a way for students to confront misinformation and better understand the issues being raised. “Fake news is still rampant in social media,” she said, adding that students should participate in organizations and mobilizations so they can better understand what they are fighting for and what their rights are.

“We are here to speak up for the issues that are happening in our country,” Bitar said.

For them, remembering Martial Law means more than recalling what happened 54 years ago. (Reposted by Bulatlat) (AMU, DAA)

author: ACG
title: Pre-budget protest.
content:
An ACG supporter writes:


Donald Trump visited Ireland recently. It was a two-day visit so he could play golf.

The estimated cost to the Irish taxpayer is reported to be in excess of 20 million

Euros (Clare Echo, 6/8/26). Not surprisingly, the visit caused controversy and

resulted in mass protests. The latter is a good thing. What is strange, however, was

the lack of enthusiasm for a protest held just one week later in Dublin.


pre-budget protest


A protest was called for September 19 th in Parnell Square, Central Dublin, as a pre-Budget demonstration. The budget is due to be announced on October 6 th by Finance Minister Simon Harris on behalf of the right-wing coalition of Fianna Fail and Fine Gael. The government is sitting on a surplus, but indications are they intend to do little or nothing to help those in need of support.


There are a number of basic issues that highlight a social crisis in the 26 Counties. A big one is housing. Social housing is no longer being built people are waiting years on lists and private landlords are allowed to get away with exorbitant rents. It is not unusual for people to pay 40 or 50% of their income on rent. That’s if you can actually find somewhere in the first place. Many young people are living in the bedrooms they grew up in, since availability is as much a problem as affordability.

Outright homelessness is on the rise too. The Department of Housing figures show

that those in emergency housing increased 9.1% over the year to July 2026 (RTE

28/8/26). Among those was a 16% increase in families (Focus Ireland 28/8/26).

The problem does not only occur on a national level. The grassroots housing

campaign group Community Action Tenants’ Union (CATU) is battling against Dublin

City Council. Council executives have increased rents for tenants in public housing,

the excuse being that there isn’t money to keep public housing in reasonable

condition, so it will have to come out of rent increases. The increase voted on in April

offers no exemptions for pensioners, people on welfare, or disability recipients. For

many of those groups dependent on fixed incomes, any increase will further diminish

their quality of life.


Besides housing, another concern is basic resource infrastructure. Due to extremely

hot weather conditions, a hosepipe ban was enforced between July and the middle

of September in the Greater Dublin Area, and parts of Wexford, Wicklow, Meath,

Kildare and south Tipperary.


Uisce Eireann (UE) is the state-owned company that was responsible for overseeing

the ban. UE declared the prohibition “…for activities including watering gardens,

washing private vehicles and leisure boats, filling domestic swimming or paddling

pools, ornamental fountains and garden ponds except where such use is required for

commercial purposes [emphasis added]”, (RTE, 22/7/26). In other words, business

got a pass and the average person had to toe the line.


Although UE is a state company, it is in fact structured as a commercial semi-state

company with share holders. The two shareholders are government ministers. It is

clear from all this whose interests are seen to take priority. It is not the people at the

bottom.


Oplus_131104


In addition, electricity prices are rising. Several suppliers have announced increases,

with some already taking effect and others about to. For example, SSE Airtricity is

increasing electricity rates by 9.4% from October 5 th , with the typical bill rising by

about 8.9% or 172 Euros a year (The Irish Times, 4/9/26). Another is Pinergy, which

imposed a 7.6% increase (RTE 14/8/26). The result is on a straight Euro-per-kWh

measure, Ireland now has the highest electricity costs in the European Union (EU), at about 40% above the EU average! (ec.europa.eu). While the average person is clearly struggling to pay these increases, data centres and big tech companies (with the latter only paying 12.5% tax) pay wholesale rates for their water and electricity, while using a huge percentage of the national consumption. Its not too hard to see who the state favours.


Examples could be multiplied across various other aspects of the cost-of-living crisis.

One such being a 15% increase in public transport, announced to take place from

January (thejournal.ie 3/9/26).Many working people rely on buses and trains to

commute to work, and such increases only add to the burden we face. Anyway it

title: Gaziantep'te 15 yıl önce işlenen cinayete ilişkin 10 gözaltı
content:
Antep’in Beybahçe Mahallesi'nde 3 Ocak 2011'de Mehmet Kaya, sokakta kimliği belirsiz kişiler tarafından silahla vuruldu. Olayın ardından şüpheliler kaçarken, Kaya otopsi işlemlerinin ardından toprağa verildi. Olayla ilgili gözaltına alınan C.Ç., E.Ç., M.Ç., O.Ç. ve K.Ç. savcılık ifadelerinin ardından serbest bırakılırken, O.Ç. adli kontrol şartı ile serbest bırakıldı.

Gaziantep Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı koordinesinde, Gaziantep İl Emniyet Müdürlüğü Cinayet Büro Amirliği'nce yeniden araştırma yapıldı. Genişletilmiş HTS analizleri ile teknik ve fiziki takip çalışmaları neticesinde O.Ç., C.Ç., E.Ç., O.Ç., M.Ç., K.Ç., S.Ç., H.Y., M.Ç. ve S.Ç. şüpheli olarak tespit edildi. Şüpheliler, 2 gün önce sabah saatlerinde Gaziantep, Şanlıurfa ve Antalya'da asayiş, özel harekat ve insansız hava araçları amirliği ekipleri tarafından yapılan eş zamanlı operasyonla yakalandı.

Olayla ilgili soruşturma sürerken, operasyona ilişkin detayları da Adalet Bakanı Akın Gürlek paylaştı. Bakan Gürlek, sosyal medya hesabından yaptığı paylaşımda, "Gaziantep'te 3 Ocak 2011 tarihinde silahlı saldırı sonucu hayatını kaybeden Mehmet Kaya'nın öldürülmesine ilişkin dosya yeniden ve bütün yönleriyle incelendi. HTS kayıtları genişletilerek yeniden analiz edildi. Tanık anlatımları, baz sinyal bilgileri, teşhis tutanakları ve şüpheli ifadelerindeki çelişkiler birlikte değerlendirildi. Bazı şüphelilerin olay günü Mehmet Kaya'yı takip ettikleri ve olay çevresinde gözetleme faaliyetinde bulundukları tespit edildi. Gaziantep Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığımızın koordinesinde Gaziantep, Şanlıurfa ve Antalya’da gerçekleştirilen eş zamanlı operasyonlarda olayla bağlantılı olduğu değerlendirilen 10 şüpheli yakalanarak gözaltına alındı" dedi.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Unknown
title: « J'ai voulu en finir » - Lettre d'un prisonnier de Moulins-Yzeure
content:
M.C. Moulins-Yzeure 2026


Ce soir je prend mon stylo car je me sens prêt à vous raconter la soirée où j'ai voulu me « pendre »… Depuis quelques temps, la pénitentiaire s'acharne sur moi. Ils m'interdisent la douche l'après-midi, ils ne veulent pas me sortir de la « gestion individuelle ». Ils me refusent des permis de visite et me poussent à l'extrême… Le suicide est mal vu chez les détenu(e)s, c'est un signe de faiblesse… Un soir, après une journée bien chargée en embrouille avec les matons, j'ai pris un drap et j'ai préparé un noeud coulant… J'ai passé la journée à me défoncer au schitt pour ne pas avoir trop de réaction de survie… J'ai accroché le nœud coulant au plafond, je me suis posé et roulé un gros cône. Je regardais la corde pendre. J'en avais tellement marre de l'acharnement de l'A.P.* que j'ai pensé que le seul moyen d'arrêter toute cette merde c'est de me foutre en l'air… J'ai fumé à mort, fais un café, mis du son, bouché mon œilleton puis je suis monté sur la chaise et passé la corde autour du cou… J'ai fini mon cône puis j'ai fait tombé la chaise… Je suis facilement resté suspendu 2 minutes. Je vous avoue que le schitt n'a plus fait effet et la peur et les regrets ont pris le dessus… Quand le drap a lâché je suis tombé au sol et j'ai chialé, chialé parce que je me suis rendu compte que l'A.P. a failli m'avoir et j'aurais fait souffrir mes proches !! Maintenant je peux vous assurer que je ne ferai plus de tentative de suicide...


Mon geste n'était pas une faiblesse, juste un ras-le-bol !!! Plus d'une décennie que je suis incarcéré sans être passé aux assises… Remarques + que racistes et patriarcales, accès + que limité aux douches, tellement, que je me lave en cellule dans un seau !!! Palpé à chaque sortie de ma cellule, même pour prendre le repas et menotté pour aller l'infirmerie !!! Tout est fait pour que je me sens plus bas que terre… Mes journées en détention sont humiliantes, ils ne peuvent même pas ouvrir ma cellule si ils ne sont pas 3 matons + 1 gradé !!! Je ne suis plus un humain, je suis une bête, une chose, que l'on baillonne et menotte… Mes proches sont la pour moi, leur soutien est vital, leur amour et amitié pour moi me donne la force de continuer à tenir et le courage pour parler de cette soirée sombre… Il faut que ce sujet sorte de l'ombre, si un être humain se fout en l'air en prison c'est forcément que quelque-chose ne va pas !!! On a été privé de liberté. On nous a pas condamné à être torturé et à perdre notre dignité et humanité !!!! J'avais 22 ans quand je suis entré en prison, j'avais encore des rêves, je rigolais tout les jours. Aujourd'hui j'ai 37 ans, je ne suis toujours pas sorti de prison et mes rêves se sont envolés. J'ai une haine incroyable contre ce système archaïque et je ne rigole plus tous les jours… A chaque journée qui commence, je me demande quelle dinguerie ils me réservent… Le seul moment où je me sens un peu tranquille, c'est la nuit. Les matons peuvent pas ouvrir la porte sauf en cas d'urgence donc j'ai un semblant de tranquillité…


Voilà, à toutes et tous, sachez que même si la vie est dure, elle mérite que l'on se batte pour elle…


Je remercie mes proches pour leur soutien,


Merci à vous, je vous aime et vous dis à bientôt dehors…


Y'a pas d'arrangement !!


ON LACHE RIEN


ACAB


1312

author: Melanie Lübbert
title: Früher hatte Überwachung noch ein Geräusch
content:
Die BigBrotherAwards 2026 sind verliehen. Eine volle Hechelei, viel Applaus und ein Abend, der gezeigt hat: Wir sind viele, die Überwachung und Datenklau nicht einfach hinnehmen.

„Früher hatte Überwachung noch ein Geräusch.“

Mit diesen Worten eröffnete padeluun die BigBrotherAwards 2026. In seinem Poetry Slam nahm er uns mit durch Jahrzehnte der Überwachung und der Verstöße gegen unsere Grundrechte. Früher war Überwachung oft noch sicht- und hörbar: Kameras klickten, Tonbänder liefen, Geräte surrten und ratterten. Heute geschieht vieles digital, automatisiert und nahezu geräuschlos im Hintergrund.

Umso wichtiger ist es, diese Eingriffe sichtbar zu machen und die Verantwortlichen beim Namen zu nennen. padeluuns Appell am Ende:

„Deshalb nennen wir Namen. Und genau deshalb gibt es Digitalcourage und die BigBrotherAwards.“

Der Funke sprang über. Der Saal in der Hechelei war voll, die Laudationes bekamen viel Applaus und auch nach dem Ende der Gala gingen die Gespräche weiter.

Die BigBrotherAwards machen sichtbar, was sonst schnell abstrakt bleibt: Überwachung, Datenmissbrauch und der Abbau digitaler Grundrechte haben Verantwortliche. Und es lohnt sich, genau hinzuschauen und sie beim Namen zu nennen.

Moderator Ralph Caspers führte auch in diesem Jahr mit viel Charme durch den Abend. Besonders begeistert haben uns wieder die Teckids. In ihrem eigenen Beitrag kritisierten sie ein pauschales Social-Media-Verbot für junge Menschen und machten deutlich: Statt digitaler Aufenthaltsverbote braucht es sichere Räume, digitale Mündigkeit und freie Alternativen.

Auch weit über die Hechelei hinaus wurden die BigBrotherAwards verfolgt: In 23 Städten in ganz Deutschland fanden Public Viewings statt. Auch die Medienresonanz war groß: Der WDR schaltete live von der Gala und berichtete über die Preisträger. Auch Süddeutsche Zeitung, Welt, Stern, netzpolitik.org, taz und Heise griffen die BigBrotherAwards auf. Selbst Stiftung Warentest berichtete über die Auszeichnung von Fielmann und Apollo Optik.

Hier finden Sie laufend aktualisiert alle Medienberichte: bigbrotherawards.de/2026/medienberichte

Das Video der Gala, sowie Fotos und alle Laudationes als Texte finden Sie unter bigbrotherawards.de/2026. Oder auf Englisch hier: bigbrotherawards.de/en/2026.

Behörden & Verwaltung: Bundesinnenminister Alexander Dobrindt für die geplante Einführung der Steuer-ID als einheitliches Personenkennzeichen im Zuge der Registermodernisierung.

Technik: Fielmann und Apollo Optik für den Verkauf von Metas Smart Glasses und damit für die Normalisierung von heimlichem Filmen und Abhören im Alltag.

Europa: die EU-Kommission für den „Digitalen Omnibus", der den europäischen Datenschutz unter dem Deckmantel der "Vereinfachung" aushöhlt.

Zivilgesellschaft: das Landeskirchenamt der Nordkirche für den Zwangseinsatz von Microsoft 365 für alle Kirchengemeinden.

Präventiv: die Deutsche Telekom AG für die geplante Fusion mit T-Mobile US, die US-Geheimdiensten den Zugriff auf deutsche Kommunikationsdaten erlauben könnte.

Wir freuen uns über Spenden und neue Mitglieder.

Wir sind erschöpft und glücklich.

Und wieder einmal merken wir nach so einem Abend, wie viel Arbeit darin steckt: monatelange Recherchen, juristische Prüfungen, Laudationes, Bühne, Technik und Livestream. Mit der Preisverleihung ist diese Arbeit nicht vorbei. An den Themen und den ausgezeichneten Fällen bleiben wir dran.

Vielen Dank an alle, die die BigBrotherAwards möglich gemacht haben: die Jury, die Teckids, das Digitalcourage-Team, die vielen Ehrenamtlichen, unsere Partnerorganisationen und Dienstleister.innen, alle Menschen, die Public Viewings organisiert haben, und natürlich unsere Mitglieder, Fördermitglieder, Spenderinnen und Spender.

author: David Greene
title: EFF to Court: Trump's Use of Truth Social's Pay-To-See-Posts-First Scheme Violates Americans' 1st Amendment Equal Access Rights
content:
EFF legal intern Simar Kaur also contributed to this article.


Americans’ First Amendment right to equal access to official government statements is violated by the Trump administration’s use of Truth Social’s preferential treatment scheme, which blocks people who won’t pay Trump’s company up to $100,000 a month early access to government news, EFF

told a federal court.

The First Amendment guarantees that members of the public have equal access to public officials’ public comments, we reminded the court.

EFF filed an

amicus brief

 in support of

a motion for a preliminary injunction

 in the

lawsuit

 filed by The Intercept Media and the Freedom of the Press Foundation against

 President Trump

 and other administration officials. The lawsuit challenges their use of Truth Social as their primary social media method of making official announcements when that platform provides people who pay a fee for early access to such posts. 

Trump uses his Truth Social account as his primary means of communicating with the public, including to announce military operations and ceasefires, foreign and domestic policy, and the removal and appointment of heads of federal agencies. Earlier in the year, Trump Media, which owns Truth Social,

announced “Truth API,”


a service that provides investors early access to “market-moving” messages from the president and other high-ranking officials for a fee of up to $100,000 per month.

The plaintiffs, the Freedom of the Press Foundation and The Intercept, contend that the president and other officials’ preferred use of Truth Social with this service violates the First and Fifth Amendments of the Constitution. The plaintiffs are asking the court to immediately prevent the president from posting on Truth Social in a manner that allows him to profit from selling early access to government information.

EFF’s amicus makes two main points.

First, the brief establishes that social media is pervasively used by government officials and agencies as a medium for official communication with the public, including to disseminate critical public safety information and make official announcements.

Second, the brief explains that the challenged practice violates the First Amendment, which guarantees a right to access public officials’ public comments on equal terms with other members of the press and public. Giving some people preferential access must at a minimum be reasonably justified to satisfy First Amendment scrutiny, a test the administration does not meet.

Lining the president and his company's pockets is not a legitimate government interest for restricting timely access to the government's statements. Further, the fact that the public could ultimately access the information from other, less direct channels does not eliminate the need for First Amendment scrutiny; mere delays in timely access still trigger First Amendment scrutiny.

EFF has been advancing the First Amendment right of equal access to government’s public social media posts

since at least 2018

. We’ve argued that the right of equal access, which is well established in offline contexts, must apply to official government social media posts as well. This case presents an excellent opportunity for a court to directly adopt that position.

author: Cody Bloomfield
title: This Group Made Tech to Protect Users’ Privacy. Trump Labeled Them Terrorists.
content:
Trump’s war on the left is coming for anti-surveillance technology providers.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

When the government puts a target on your back, every corner of online organizing becomes a puzzle. How do you ensure that your emails are private, when Google will hand over the contents of your emails to prosecutors, sometimes without ever notifying you? How do you keep your comrades informed, when maintaining an email list poses a security risk? How do you share information online without compromising the security of your web visitors?

Until September 6, the Autistici/Inventati (A/I) Collective provided privacy-focused digital infrastructure that allowed aligned groups around the world to evade government surveillance. Under siege, groups from Hamas to the Seattle Anarchist Book Fair sought refuge from the prying eyes of three-letter agencies through the use of A/I Collective email addresses, websites, mailing lists, and blogs. The users of A/I Collective technology were no strangers to the United States counterterrorism apparatus, but on August 26, 2026, the Trump administration took the unusual escalatory step of listing the technology provider itself as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist organization.

Legal uncertainty and disruption ensued immediately after the designation. The sanctions framework maps far more cleanly onto groups directly engaged in violence than it does onto a group providing anti-surveillance technology. Under the post-9/11 executive order establishing the Specially Designated Global Terrorist list, fundraising for ISIS or holding joint press conferences with al-Qaeda is verboten. But could posting on blogs hosted by the A/I Collective trigger a $1 million fine and 20 years of imprisonment? Official communications provide little assistance; the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control FAQ unhelpfully states that the exchange of information may be either blocked or exempt.

In a press release, the State Department pointed to the A/I Collective’s vetting of users for “ideological affinity,” folding the targeting of the organization into the enforcement of Donald Trump’s National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 (NSPM-7), which has initiated a crackdown on the global left. Civil society groups immediately noted the escalation into targeting not only those accused of violence, but their purported backers. “The designation of A/I Collective is significant because Treasury is applying counterterrorism sanctions not only to organizations it alleges engage directly in violence, but also to entities it characterizes as providing enabling infrastructure to designated or terrorist-linked groups…[G]roups and individuals that rely on the A/I Collective’s infrastructure may now need to assess whether continued use creates sanctions exposure,” wrote the Charity & Security Network, a coalition that has helped nonprofits navigate sanctions risk since 2009.

While users of A/I Collective services struggled to interpret the sanctions, the hammer came down immediately on the volunteer collective. Within 48 hours of the designation, the United States-based holder of the autistici.org domain shuttered the website, leaving A/I Collective to flee to an alternate domain. The Italian Banca Etica suspended the bank account the volunteer collective used to collect donations, citing sanctions risk. Backed into a corner, with no way to protect users and collect the donations needed to fund its €13,000 annual budget, the A/I Collective announced the shutdown of all of its services on September 6, 2026. In a statement, the A/I Collective wrote: “The possibility that our work may cause legal and financial consequences to those who are close to us — or even only have something to do with us — leaves us no choice.” On September 20, an estimated 10,000 NoBlogs sites went dark, stranding the radical activists who used the A/I Collective-hosted blogging platform to share everything from zines to direct-action tactical communiques.

With prosecutors on the hunt for novel methods to weave together conspiracy charges against anarchists and other left movements, the A/I Collective’s assessment may unfortunately prove correct. author: EDRi
title: Simplification for whom? Open letter to EU Member States to uphold GDPR protections in Digital Omnibus on Data
content:
Over the past months, the European Commission's Digital Omnibus on Data has turned into a wider discussion about how much protection the data – and with it, the rights – of people in the EU should receive in the name of AI, innovation and competitiveness. That discussion has now reached a critical stage in the Council.

EU governments are now discussing critical issues like whether data should sometimes fall outside the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) depending on who holds the data, whether AI deserves special treatment when companies want to reuse personal data, and whether people should receive less information about how their data are used. The Irish Presidency’s compromise of 3 September has raised serious concerns across the board. A revised text circulated on 21 September seemingly attempted at improving some parts of it, but leaves the most fundamental questions unresolved. Just as the Commission’s Proposal, this is deregulation of substance, not simply less paperwork, it is happening very quickly, and the legal drafting is quite worrying.

The Council has stepped back from directly rewriting the GDPR’s definition of ‘personal data,’ and this may sound reassuring. But it is not: the new Article 25a and the accompanying Recitals 27 still risk changing the answer to the same basic question: when does the GDPR apply?

To understand why, it helps to distinguish pseudonymisation from anonymisation. Pseudonymisation means replacing obvious identifiers, such as a name, with something else, like a code or an ID number. That can make data safer, because the information linking the code back to the person is kept separately. But the person is still there behind the code, and the data, together with the rights attached to them, are still meant to remain protected.

This is not an abstract scenario. Much of today’s online tracking already works through pseudonymous identifiers rather than people’s names. Cookie IDs, advertising IDs, device identifiers and similar codes are used to recognise people over time, link their behaviour across services, build profiles and decide what content, prices or adverts they see. In many contexts, knowing that someone is ‘User 15051948’ is actually more useful for tracking and targeting them than knowing their name.

Anonymisation is different. Data are anonymous only when a person can no longer realistically be identified from them, including by combining them with other information that is reasonably available. Anonymous data fall outside the GDPR. Pseudonymised data do not simply become anonymous because one company cannot immediately put a name to the person.

The Council’s approach risks blurring exactly that line, between data that are still being used to single out and act on a person, and data that are genuinely anonymous. Under Article 25a, the same pseudonymised data could be treated as personal data for one actor but as non-personal data for another if that actor is considered unable to identify the person. In practice, this can produce something very close to narrowing the definition of personal data itself. That creates two problems.

The first issue is about rights. If a company treats the data as outside the GDPR, many of the protections attached to the GDPR may disappear with it: the duty to keep data secure, people’s right to know how data are used, the right to access or correct them, or to object to certain uses.

The second is about legal certainty. Digital data rarely sit with one company. They move through long chains of service providers, advertisers, analytics companies, cloud providers and data brokers that disproportionately depend on distributed data processing: different actors hold different pieces of information (all of them surely pseudonymised) and have different technical capabilities. So the legal status of the same dataset will change depending on who is holding it at a given moment. That means companies, regulators and individuals may first have to work out who can identify whom, with which data and at which point in the chain, before they can even answer the basic question of whether the GDPR applies. And there is an obvious incentive problem here: actors already argue that they are not responsible because they cannot themselves identify the person behind an identifier, or because another actor in the chain holds the information needed to do so. Article 25a risks giving those arguments considerably more legal weight.

For a law supposedly …
