author: CMI Argentina
title: “La carne que falta en los comedores se la robaron en la Quinta de Olivos”
content:
Tras difundirse la denuncia de un nuevo hecho de corrupción del gobierno nacional de ultraderecha, en esta oportunidad en relación al desvío de alimentos comprados por el Estado por parte de allegados a los hermanos Milei, organizaciones sociales se manifestaron en la puerta de la residencia oficial. Reclamaron el restablecimiento del Programa Volver al Trabajo y la entrega inmediata de insumos para los barrios populares.


Foto: Prensa CCC


La Unión de Trabajadores y Trabajadoras de la Economía Popular (UTEP) junto a la CCC y otras organizaciones de desocupados y precarizados marcharon a la Quinta de Olivos para denunciar la corrupción en la gestión de alimentos oficiales y exigir la reinstalación del Programa Volver al Trabajo (VAT) y la entrega inmediata de insumos para los barrios populares.


“A los barrios les niegan la comida y en la quinta se la roban”, sostiene una de las consignas de la jornada de protesta.


https://argentina.indymedia.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/utep.mp4


Video: Corresponsal popular


Corrupción con alimentos


La diputada nacional ex mileísta, Marcela Pagano, denunció recientemente un esquema de corrupción en la Quinta de Olivos con irregularidades en la compra de alimentos. La legisladora pidió investigar si un catering privado perteneciente a María Belén Agudiez, la ex subsecretaria de Planificación General eyectada tras estallar el escándalo y muy cercana a Karina Milei, utilizó personal e insumos pagados por el Estado.


“La protesta cobra mayor gravedad tras la difusión del último índice de pobreza del INDEC correspondiente al primer semestre”, señaló la UTEP mediante un comunicado que remarcó que las cifras oficiales se quedan cortas frente a la realidad de los barrios, donde las familias deben endeudarse para comprar alimentos y hacer frente a aumentos insostenibles en servicios y alquileres.


Foto: Prensa CCC


“La carne y la comida que falta en nuestros comedores son más de 500 millones que se los chorearon acá en Olivos con Karina Milei a la cabeza través de su conchabo de las 29 toneladas de carne que licitó desde su área”, apuntó Johana Duarte, Secretaria Gremial de la UTEP, en declaraciones al periódico cooperativo

Tiempo Argentino

.


“Hoy vinimos a mostrar que mientras 1/3 de la población argentina está sumergida en la absoluta pobreza, en este antro presidencial se roban la plata que debieran ir a las políticas alimentarias para quienes peor la pasan en la Argentina, millones de familias que en el mejor de los casos llegan a comer 3 comidas por semana. Denunciamos esta situación de gravedad extrema donde unos pocos se enfiestan a costa de la pobreza y la indigencia de millones de argentinos”, expresó Johana.


“Nosotros endeudados y sin garantizar la comida. Ellos derrochando ‘la del Pueblo’”, señalaron por su parte desde la Corriente Clasista y Combativa (CCC), y llamaron a “terminar con esta política de hambre, choreo y entrega nacional para que florezca otra que resuelva Pan, Tierra, Techo y Trabajo para todos y todas”.

author: Brian Bienkowski
title: Pesticide Linked to Cancer Pollutes 25 Percent of US River and Stream Miles
content:
Atrazine, which is banned in more than 60 countries, is contaminating many waterways used for drinking water.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

A cancer-linked pesticide banned in more than 60 countries around the world contaminates an estimated 25% of river and stream miles in the lower 48 US states, including many waterways used for drinking water, according to a new analysis.

The analysis from the Center for Biological Diversity builds on evidence that atrazine — which is commonly used to grow corn, soybeans, sorghum and sugarcane and is linked to dangerous health problems for people and wildlife — remains ubiquitous in US waterways, especially in farming states.

“It’s just an astounding level of contamination from just one pesticide,” said Nathan Donley, the environmental health science director at the Center for Biological Diversity.

The findings come as the Trump administration re-evaluates atrazine’s registration and signals its support for continued use, including by dismissing research by international cancer experts on links between cancer and atrazine late last year.

Atrazine is the second most widely used herbicide in the US after glyphosate. US farmers apply roughly 70 million pounds of the pesticide to their fields every year, according to US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) estimates. Exposure has been linked to birth defects, low birth weights, hormone disruption, some cancers and immune system problems. It is also considered an endocrine disruptor, meaning it can interfere with the human hormone system.

The Center for Biological Diversity used EPA data focused on waterways in the lower 48 states, and examined the prevalence of atrazine at levels that exceeded the EPA’s threshold for harm to river ecosystems, which is 9.7 parts per billion (ppb). The agency’s maximum contaminant level for drinking water, by comparison, is 3 ppb.

The analysis showed watersheds that were contaminated with atrazine at levels above 9.7 ppb encompassed 258,451,869 acres out of a total of 1,928,393,471 acres (13%) in the continental US.

The analysis found contamination is highly concentrated in a few “hotspots” — the Chesapeake Bay, Midwest Corn Belt, Lake Okeechobee, the Lower Mississippi River and the Texas Gulf Coast — and that roughly 22% of the country’s drinking water facilities get water from surface water in rivers that were found contaminated.

Dana Kolpin, a research hydrologist with the US Geological Survey (USGS), said that Midwest farming states have been the geographic “bullseye” for decades of atrazine pollution, and the highest levels are seen after a “spring flush.”

“Farmers use the compound in spring, it rains, and then it flushes into the streams — this is the driving force of why we find it in rivers,” he said. The new analyses confirmed this runoff pollution problem persists in the Corn Belt — Kansas, Nebraska, Iowa, Missouri, Illinois, Indiana and Ohio — where more than two thirds of those states’ river miles had elevated levels of atrazine. Kolpin said the presence of atrazine in water often signals even more pesticide pollution.

“Pesticides are kind of like cockroaches — if you find one you’ll likely find a whole bunch,” he said.

A USGS study on pesticides in US rivers published in May also found that atrazine was one of “the greatest threats to surface water availability” and that “concentrations were not shifting significantly over time.”

“We’ve known about this problem for decades,” Donley said. “The EPA has shown it is just utterly incapable of putting in place protections that make any meaningful change when it comes to atrazine water contamination in this country.”

The EPA is conducting a registration review of atrazine, but has signaled its intent to reapprove. In December 2025 the agency brushed off a lengthy scientific review from the World Health Organization’s International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) that determined atrazine was “probably carcinogenic to humans.”

The IARC cited evidence in human, animal and mechanistic studies leading to its conclusions, including research linking the chemical to non-Hodgkin lymphoma in people. IARC said there was “strong” evidence in mechanistic studies showing atrazine exhibits key characteristics of carcinogens, including inflammation, oxidative stress and cell death.

author: David Swanson
title: November 20: Support Student Strike for Peace
content:
By

STOP Rearm Europe

, September 25, 2026


Around 20 November 2026, we call on you to take action. That day, students across Europe will go on an

International Youth Strike

, rallying behind Fight For Our Future, Not Their Wars. In the days before and after, mobilisations, demonstrations and actions are being organised in cities across the continent. Together we are mobilising for Welfare, not Warfare.


Army adverts on every screen. Officers in our classrooms. Jobseekers steered towards the barracks. Mounting pressure on women and girls to enlist. Young men and boys offered a rifle instead of a future. Refugees, deserters and conscientious objectors threatened with being sent back to the front. Hospitals and schools cut to pay for tanks. Billions of our money poured into militarising our borders, our universities and our economies.


We reject the militarisation of our societies and support the young people who are refusing it. Thousands of high school and university students across Europe are rising up to refuse militarisation and the return of conscription. On 20 November, they will embark on the

first international youth strike and mobilisation

.


We call on you to join this resistance.


We mobilise because:


Wars are multiplying and deepening. Genocide is being normalised, civilian infrastructure has become a routine target, and international institutions stand paralysed. Long-standing taboos are unravelling: European governments are withdrawing from the Mine Ban Treaty and ignoring the Arms Trade Treaty. The rule of law is giving way to the rule of force.


Wars deepen the cost-of-living crisis, as the US–Israeli attack on Iran made painfully clear. Our governments back that war, even as it hurts people across the world, Europe included.


Nearly 20 million children in the EU – one in four – live at risk of poverty or social exclusion. Meanwhile, governments have committed to military spending that the EU’s own Defence Commissioner, Andrius Kubilius, puts at €7 trillion by 2035.


Housing, healthcare, diplomacy and the reindustrialisation needed for a just transition are all being deprioritised. Governments have no plan to deal with worsening heatwaves, floods and wildfires – and show no interest in pathways to peace and climate justice.


Militarisation curtails freedom. It criminalises those who dare to criticise the rush to war, war crimes and complicity in genocides. Dissent is being punished through EU sanctions imposed without trial.


The public is made to fear migrants and foreign enemies, pitting working people against each other. Yet those on opposite sides of a front line have more in common with one another than with the governments that send them to the battlefield, or the companies that profit from war, borders and surveillance.


Welfare, not Warfare: The Case for a Just Transition


The trillions earmarked for militarised security will leave us staring down the barrel of a gun and indebted to global financiers. What we need instead is a democratic plan for a just transition in Europe, built on global solidarity and centred on care: a reindustrialisation programme that creates secure jobs with good working conditions, and an economy directed towards the common good and the protection of nature.


This must go hand in hand with a non-aligned foreign policy that resolves conflicts through diplomacy, upholds international law and human rights, and builds common security for all: security with our neighbours, not against them.


This is why we are calling on social movements, trade unions, civil society organisations, independent media, political forces and parliamentarians to endorse this call, mobilise their members, and join us in the streets in the days around 20 November demanding Welfare, not Warfare.


For additional information, please contact: action@stoprearm.org

To add your mobilisation to the Europe-wide calendar, please visit:

https://calendar.stoprearm.org/events/insert.php


To view mobilisations around 20 November, navigate to:

https://calendar.stoprearm.org/events/

author: CMI Argentina
title: Senado: LLA y aliados convirtieron en ley la quita de subsidios al gas a unos 5 millones de personas
content:
Con esto pierden sus descuentos zonas de las provincias de Buenos Aires, Córdoba, Santa Fe, Mendoza, Salta, San Juan, San Luis, Jujuy y La Rioja que fueron agregadas por ley en 2021 al régimen de zona fría.


Lo mantendrán, pero sólo en el precio del gas y no en el resto de los cargos de la boleta, las provincias de Ushuaia, Santa Cruz, Chubut, Río Negro, Neuquén y La Pampa, más Malargüe en Mendoza y la Puna Jujeña.


La senadora radical por Mendoza Mariana Juri aseguró que con esto se genera más inequidad: “En Mendoza el gas en invierno no es un lujo ni un confort prescindible, es una necesidad vital de subsistencia y hoy sin fundamentos técnicos nos están metiendo la mano en el bolsillo de los mendocinos”.


El senador radical por la provincia de Buenos Aires Maximiliano Abad recalcó que incluso las zonas que mantendrán los subsidios por zona fría sufrirán fuertes subas ya que el descuento se limitará al precio del gas y no al resto de los cargos de la boleta, como la distribución.


“El subsidio que se va a dar a partir de la sanción de esta ley es sobre un porcentaje y un componente de la boleta, ese componente es el valor del gas, no se contempla ni la distribución ni los impuestos”.


Y remarcó: “estando en zona fría o no las boletas se van a disparar y para muchos ciudadanos va a ser inalcanzable poder pagarlas”.


Por esta modificación de los subsidios al consumo de gas más de 3 millones de personas en el país perderán todo subsidio a la boleta de gas.

author: Acratosaurio rex
title: El mito del buen alcalde, que manda obedeciendo
content:
El alcalde del cuadro se hizo anarquista. El de la camisa a cuadros, aún no sabemos.

Como estos tiempos son de mitos, voy a volver a divagar sobre el mito de las elecciones democráticas. Por echar el rato. Quienes desde la izquierda e incluso desde posiciones libertarias, intentan cambiar las cosas, y creen en ese mito… ¿Qué tenemos de actualidad?

En 2021 la sección sindical de CC.OO. en el Ayuntamiento de Cádiz, puso en conocimiento del fiscal de por allí, presuntas irregularidades cometidas por el alcalde José María González apodado el «Kichi». Admirador de Fermín Salvochea hasta el punto de poner su retrato en su despacho.

Breve puesta en escena: Kichi fue aupado a la alcaldía por la plataforma Por Cádiz Sí Se Puede (en minoría en 2015), y posteriormente en 2019 por Adelante Cádiz (a uno de mayoría absoluta). Eran candidaturas que surgieron con el impulso de Podemos, aunque no eran Podemos. Estas candidaturas pretendían devolver Cádiz a los ciudadanos, mandar obedeciendo… No entro en detalles que si no aburro demasiado.

Resulta que Kichi entra en el Ayuntamiento a mandar obedeciendo, tras 20 años de gobiernos del PP con Teófila Martínez al mando. Corramos un tupido velo sobre Teófila, que es o era una criatura indescriptible. He aquí a Kichi, entrando en el Ayuntamiento, donde se encuentra: funcionarios, secretario, interventor, contratación, abogados, técnicos, empresas municipales y procedimientos administrativos. Gente que ha entrado bajo el gobierno del PP.

Y con ellos los sindicatos representativos: seis. Autonomía Obrera con 7 en Junta de Personal (funcionarios) y 1 en el Comité de Empresa (laborales). Policías y bomberos, UGT, CSIF. Y Comisiones Obreras, que abre la denuncia, tiene 3 en junta y 2 en Comité.

Bueno, ese es el escenario. Llega Kichi al Ayuntamiento, donde hay una red clientelar de 20 años de PP, con favores múltiples a personas de ahí dentro. Es profesor de Historia en un instituto. Y no tiene santa puta idea de cómo funciona un ayuntamiento y qué leyes se aplican. ¿Qué intenta hacer, aparte de ser simpático con todo dios? Lo que puede hacer un edil honrado: que se cumpla la ley. Y es que no se puede salir de ese guión, porque el interventor, el servicio jurídico, el secretario/a, los/las funcionarios, le van a poner miles de pegas. Y en cuanto se descuide le van a acusar de prevaricar: actuar a sabiendas en contra de la ley.

¿Cómo se enfrenta a este dilema Kichi, de ser un alcalde ignorante? Busca a un asesor jurídico técnico para cuestiones de contratación y política social. Dos temas delicados. Lo paga con el dinero de su coalición entre 2018 y 2019. El asesor tiene un buen perfil jurídico, se pone manos a la obra. Y genera la suficiente molestia, pidiendo papeles, señalando correcciones, y metiendo las narices aquí y allí, como para que en 2021, CC.OO. denuncie al asesor por prevaricación administrativa y revelación de secretos. Actualmente le piden a Kichi 18 años de inhabilitación y 10.800 euros de multa. Sin que haya contratos fraudulentos, sin que se haya quedado con dinero, volviendo a su puesto de trabajo como profesor, ¡de historia!, ¿no aprendiste algo? con su sueldo pelado= Inhabilitación, y multazo.

O sea, en fin, un pringao, Kichi, que llega a alcalde, y quiere ser honrado… ¿Qué se piensa? ¿Que va a mandar obedeciendo? ¿Que puede tener a un tío que no es funcionario, ni es de CC.OO., ni del PP, ni del PSOE, fisgoneando en el papeleo y contradiciendo al abogado del ayuntamiento? Denuncia al canto.

En resumen: ¿qué fue lo que consiguió Kichi en sus años de mandato para el pueblo de Cái?

Aplíquese el cuento. O el Mito democrático.

author: Unknown
title: BM, yükselen okyanusların ülkeleri örteceği geleceğe hazırlanıyor: Ada ülkeleri için yeni uluslararası hukuk ilkesi
content:
Birleşmiş Milletler (BM) Genel Kurulu, yükselen denizlerin yalnızca evleri ve kentleri değil, devletlerin kendilerini de ortadan kaldırabilme olasılığı karşısında uluslararası hukukun karşı karşıya kaldığı soruyu ele aldı: Bir ülkenin toprağı yaşanamaz hale gelir ya da okyanusun altında kalırsa o ülke hâlâ bir devlet midir?


Genel Kurul, 24 Eylül Perşembe günü New York'ta düzenlenen "Deniz Seviyesinin Yükselmesinin Yol Açtığı Varoluşsal Tehditler Üst Düzey Toplantısı"nda kabul ettiği siyasi bildirgeyle, bu ülkelerin devlet olma statüsünün ve egemenliğinin sürekliliğinin korunması yönünde ortak irade ortaya koydu. Bildirge, yükselen deniz seviyelerinin özellikle alçak rakımlı küçük ada devletleri için yarattığı tehdidi yalnızca bir çevre sorunu değil, egemenlik, yurttaşlık, kendi kaderini tayin hakkı, yerinden edilme ve insan hakları sorunu olarak da ele aldı. 


Tehlike Dakka'dan New York'a kadar uzanıyor


BM Genel Kurulu Başkanı Khalilur Rahman toplantının açılışında tehlikenin küçük ada devletleriyle sınırlı olmadığını vurguladı. Küresel ortalama deniz seviyesindeki yıllık yükselme 1993-2002 döneminde 2,1 milimetre iken 2015-2024 arasında 4,7 milimetreye çıktı. Rahman, tehdidin Marshall Adaları'ndan kendi ülkesi Bangladeş'in başkenti Dakka'ya ve toplantının yapıldığı New York'a kadar uzandığını söyledi.


Bir ülke toprağını kaybederse ne olur?


Sorunun en keskin biçimde ortaya çıktığı yerler Pasifik'teki Tuvalu, Kiribati ve Marshall Adaları. Bu ülkelerin büyük bölümü deniz seviyesinin yalnızca yaklaşık 2 metre üzerinde yer alıyor. BM, kıyıların aşınması, arazilerin su altında kalması ve giderek güçlenen fırtınaların bazı düşük rakımlı ada devletlerini kısmen, hatta tamamen yaşanamaz hale getirebileceğini belirtiyor.


Tehlike yalnız adaların bir gün bütünüyle denizin altında kalması değil. Deniz yükseldikçe yüksek gelgitler ve fırtına kabarmaları daha geniş alanları su altında bırakıyor; tuzlu su tatlı su kaynaklarına ve tarım alanlarına karışıyor; yolları, evleri ve diğer altyapıyı tehdit ediyor. Böylece, bir ada haritadan silinmeden çok önce, üzerinde sürekli ve güvenli bir yaşam sürdürmek zorlaşabiliyor.


Bu olası durum uluslararası hukukun alışılmış devlet tanımını da zorluyor. Devlet olmanın temel unsurları arasında belirli bir toprak, sürekli bir nüfus, bir hükümet ve diğer devletlerle ilişki kurabilme kapasitesi sayılıyor. Oysa, BM'nin kendi değerlendirmesine göre mevcut uluslararası hukuk araçları, deniz seviyesinin yükselmesi sonucunda toprağını kaybeden bir devletin hukuki varlığının nasıl devam edeceği sorununu açıkça düzenlemiyor.


BM'nin kabul ettiği yeni bildirge bu açıdan yaşamsal önemde. Ada devletleri yıllardır toprak kaybının devlet, yurttaşlık ve egemenlik kaybına dönüşmemesi için uluslararası güvence istiyordu. Pasifik Adaları Forumu ve Küçük Ada Devletleri İttifakı (Alliance of Small Island States - AOSIS) daha önce devlet statüsünün sürekliliği ilkesini kabul etmişti. BM Genel Kurulu kabul ettiği siyasi bildirgeyle bu yaklaşımı küresel düzeye taşıyor.


Tuvalu: Göç ederken ülkeyi korumak


Yaklaşık 10 bin nüfuslu Tuvalu, bu geleceğin bugünden görülebildiği ülkelerden biri.


Ada devleti, bir yandan kıyı koruma ve arazi yükseltme projeleriyle insanların ülkede kalmasını sağlamaya çalışırken, öte yandan nüfusunun bir bölümünün güvenli bir şekilde başka ülkelere yerleşebilmesi için hukuki yollar da oluşturuyor.


Avustralya ile Tuvalu arasında yürürlüğe giren Falepili Birliği, Tuvalu yurttaşlarına Avustralya'da yaşama, çalışma ve eğitim görme imkânı sağlayan özel bir göç yolu açtı. Ancak düzenlemenin siyasi önemi göçten daha büyük: Avustralya, iklim değişikliğinin etkileri sonucunda Tuvalu'nun fiziksel topraklarında değişiklik meydana gelse bile Tuvalu'nun devlet ve egemenliğinin devam etmesini tanıdı.


Dolayısıyla Tuvalı bir “tahliye” sürecinden geçmiyor. Ada halkı, başka yerlere yerleşmek zorunda kalsa bile ülkesini, yurttaşlığını ve siyasal varlığını kaybetmemenin güvenli yollarını arıyor.


Ada kaybolmadan hayat kaybolabilir


Deniz seviyesinin yükselmesine ilişkin haberlerde sık kullanılan “batan ülkeler” görüntüsü sorunun karmaşık niteliğini de gizleyebiliyor. Bir ülkenin bütünüyle sular altında kalması için onlarca yıl gerekebilir; buna karşılık içme suyunun tuzlanması, tarım alanlarının kullanılamaz hâle gelmesi, sürekli taşkınlar ve altyapının korunmasının giderek pahalılaşması yaşamı bir ada tamamen sular altında kalmadan çok daha önce sürdürülemez hâle getirebilir.


Bu nedenle …

author: Randi Beers
title: My travels as a small-town Inuk woman
content:
Annie Qimirpik


For someone from Kimmirut, a community of roughly 450 people, travelling out of town means getting on a plane, just like everywhere else in Nunavut.


There are no roads connecting us to the rest of the territory, let alone the rest of Canada. If you want to go somewhere else, you leave by air.


I grew up surrounded by vast landscape and in a very small population where everybody knows everybody. Often, everybody knows everybody’s business. There’s comfort in that kind of familiarity but there are also limitations. The world can feel far away.


This summer, over the course of six weeks, I travelled from six places: Iqaluit, Ottawa, Toronto, London, U.K., Clyde River and Cancun, Mexico.


Each was different and they gave me another way of looking at home.


Iqaluit was the beginning. Although I’m from Kimmirut, Iqaluit has become familiar to me the way other places haven’t. It’s still Nunavut. You see people you know, still hear Inuktitut. Still surrounded by Arctic landscape.


But it’s also a city by northern standards.


Then there’s Ottawa: my first home away from home outside of Kimmirut. Moving there was my first real experience of being away from my community and having to figure things out for myself. It was strange being somewhere I couldn’t simply walk down the street and recognize most of the people I passed. 


Then came Toronto, my first solo vacation destination when I was 18. The airport alone has more people than Kimmirut does. Toronto is a fast place and incredibly diverse but Canadian at the same time. The number of people, languages, cultures and communities was something I couldn’t help but notice.


Then I crossed the Atlantic Ocean to London. I went alone, during a heat wave, to one of the biggest cities in the world. It was terrifying. It was exhilarating. There were moments when I wondered what I got myself into, especially when I got lost, which was every outing. But there was also something liberating about realizing that I could navigate a completely unfamiliar place on my own.


I was a small-town Inuk woman from Kimmirut, thousands of kilometres from home, figuring it out as I went. 


Clyde River was different. It’s where my biological daughter is from. Seeing her after four-to-five years and feeling the relationship become closer again gave that part of my trip a meaning that I can’t really measure in kilometres.


After travelling, I didn’t experiencing Nunavut in quite the same way anymore.


Then there was Cancun, Mexico. Once again, I was somewhere completely removed from the Arctic, with a different climate, language, culture and landscape. Yet I was still carrying the North with me. That became one of the biggest things I noticed during the six weeks.


When you’re from a small community, you can sometimes become accustomed to the idea that your way of life is simply the way life is. Travelling makes that assumption harder to hold. There are so many ways to live, so many different languages, cultures and ways of understanding family, community, land and identity. 


I think Inuit should have the opportunity to experience more diversity because the rest of the world can help us understand our own place within it.


The North is its own world. It has its own realities, strengths and challenges, but somehow the further I travelled, the more I wanted to come home.


Annie Qimirpik is a writer living in Iqaluit who maintains a self-titled blog about life in the North.

author: Chris Walker
title: Processing Error Could Disenfranchise Tens of Thousands of Voters in Texas
content:
The deadline to register to vote in Texas is October 5.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

A massive backlog of voter registration applications in Texas could affect the outcome of local and state elections, including a contentious election involving a U.S. Senate seat.

Public officials in the Republican-controlled state have not yet acknowledged what the error actually is. It’s also possible that the error could have affected elections from before the primary elections in March 2026, officials have acknowledged.

“Texas county voter registrars across the state have received a flood of new voter registrations and updates to voter registration records submitted through the Texas Department of Public Safety,” said Chris McGinn, executive director of the Texas Association of County Election Officials. “Some of these submissions date as far back as October 2025.”

It’s unclear how many voters could be affected by the error. McGinn acknowledged that “counties have received anywhere from several hundred to tens of thousands of records to process.” In Bexar County alone, around 45,000 registrations that have been submitted have not yet been processed.

All 254 counties in the state appear to be affected. The Texas Secretary of State’s office alerted all counties to the issue in an email last week, writing:

Counties have alerted us to the fact that some older [Department of Public Safety] registrations are now appearing on their dashboard. We are actively investigating this issue to determine the source of these historical records.

The situation is dire, as the registration deadline for Texan voters for the upcoming general election is October 5. County officials have until October 19 to process registrations, which is the same date that early voting begins.

James Talarico, a Democrat and state representative who is running in the Senate election against State Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), called the situation “unacceptable,” and encouraged all voters to check their registration status.

“Less than two weeks before the voter registration deadline, thousands of Texans are now in the dark about their voter registration status — even more aren’t aware of this error at all,” Talarico said in a statement. “This is what a broken, corrupt political system looks like: Texans follow the rules, register to vote before the deadline, and still risk losing their God-given right to the ballot box because their government failed to do its job.”

The Senate race between Talarico and Paxton is a close one, and even a small error that goes unaddressed before the November election could affect the outcome.

A longtime Republican stronghold, Talarico is currently ahead in the polls with a slim lead against Paxton. According to an average of surveys collected by the polling aggregate site FiftyPlusOne, Talarico secures around 47.9 percent of the vote, while Paxton receives around 44.6 percent.

This September, Truthout is celebrating 25 years of publication. For over two decades, we have been a trusted source for fiercely independent journalism thanks to readers like you.

Looking to the next 25 years, we launched a special fundraising campaign. We still need to raise $16,000.

We are asking for your support at this juncture because we face greater threats than ever before in our organizational history. Trump and his MAGA allies are determined to control the information ecosystem, and movement-based organizations are subject to dangerous censorship and scrutiny.

If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work and our legacy. Anything you can do makes a difference!

author: Unknown
title: Cosenza: Basta carovita, carburante, bollette, spese
content:
Il 1 ottobre  alle ore 18 in Piazza XI Settembre a Cosenza è stata indetta una manifestazione contro il carovita. Riprendiamo il testo da

La Base.


I rincari colpiscono tutta Italia, ma non colpiscono tutti allo stesso modo.


In una terra dove il lavoro non c’è, e quando c’è è nero, precario o sottopagato, ogni aumento pesa il doppio.

Qui il pieno serve per andare a lavorare, per raggiungere un ospedale, per portare i figli a scuola, perché i servizi pubblici li hanno smantellati pezzo dopo pezzo.

Qui le bollette arrivano in case dove entra un solo stipendio, quando va bene, e fare la spesa significa scegliere cosa togliere dal carrello.


Da decenni la Calabria viene trattata come un posto da cui andarsene: ospedali chiusi, treni che non passano, giovani costretti a partire.


I rincari rischiano di essere la pietra tombale per decine di migliaia di famiglie.

Il costo della vita quotidiana è ormai l’unica spesa che prosciuga tutto il salario, mentre iniziamo a fare economia anche sui chilometri da percorrere.


Blocchiamo la spirale degli aumenti, prima che anche la vita quotidiana diventi insostenibile!


Il carovita non è una fatalità: mentre il paese si impoverisce, qualcuno sta facendo profitti record sulla nostra pelle e sulla pelle delle persone che stanno pagando con la vita le guerre dei potenti.


Non ci basta sopravvivere, vogliamo poter vivere con dignità, felici, come ogni essere umano avrebbe diritto a fare.


1 ottobre, ore 18

Piazza XI Settembre, Cosenza.


Scendiamo in piazza, perché restare in silenzio è l’unica cosa che davvero non possiamo più permetterci!

author: Marina Amaral
title: Na corrida pela notícia, imprensa entrega o “ouro” para as redes
content:
Quer receber os textos desta coluna em primeira mão no seu e-mail? Assine a Newsletter da Pública, enviada sempre às sextas-feiras, 8h. Para receber as próximas edições,

inscreva-se aqui

.


Achei muito interessante o episódio apresentado por Fábio Porchat, criado e produzido pelo podcast “Calma Urgente”, sobre as relações entre os Vorcaro, a Igreja da Lagoinha e os Bolsonaro. Mais do que as tiradas divertidas do humorista,

o que me impressionou foi a capacidade de dar sentido aos fatos, com uma narrativa acessível e precisa sobre o que significa o escândalo do Master e quem são seus reais protagonistas.  


O projeto une artistas e jornalistas e parece ter encontrado uma forma eficiente de dialogar com o público nessas eleições tão complexas, infiltradas por

recursos

 de organizações criminosas e ameaçadas por Donald Trump, aliado e beneficiário das Big Techs.


Notem: os fatos que embasam a história contada por Porchat não são “furos”, mas foram amarrados de forma a torná-los compreensíveis para o leitor sem descambar na propaganda. Talvez seja esse o motivo pelo qual o perfil “Revelando” – que divulga os episódios – tenha sido

censurado

 (e depois liberado) pela Meta quando já alcançava 6 milhões de visualizações (e o

vídeo

 5,4 milhões de views no YouTube até o momento em que escrevo, quando um novo episódio já está sendo lançado). 


O que vale uma reflexão sobre o jornalismo, sobretudo aquele que continua repetindo métodos (como os vazamentos seletivos), fontes e formatos (a notícia-mercadoria) sem compreender a mudança de seu papel no novo ecossistema informativo.


Tenho cá para mim que a expectativa dos donos das empresas jornalísticas não vai além de conseguir negociar com as Big Techs para obter pagamentos em troca das notícias que entregam de graça como combustível para as redes – pelo menos até que a inteligência artificial se encarregue de criá-las ao gosto do freguês. Afinal, não se pode esperar muito de quem não vê contradição entre defender o interesse público e lucrar com anúncios de bets – prática rejeitada por cem veículos digitais em

manifestação

 liderada pela

Agência


Pública.

 Hoje (24), o presidente Lula deve assinar uma

MP

 proibindo as bets no país. 


Para nós, jornalistas, a batalha é outra.

Se queremos cumprir nosso papel na garantia ao direito à informação da população, temos que preservar o “ouro” do jornalismo: o sentido dos fatos, o que começa pela leitura política da realidade.

 Como já dizia o mestre Cláudio Abramo: “O jornalismo não pode ser despido de opinião política. Deve-se sim ter opinião, saber onde ela começa e acaba, onde ela interfere nas coisas ou não. É preciso ter consciência. O jornalista não pode ser ingênuo, deve ser cético. Ele não pode ser impiedoso com as coisas sem um critério ético”.


Se isso já era importante há 40 anos, imagine agora em que o produto do nosso trabalho está sujeito a uma mega manipulação de significado e sentido, a depender de quem se aproveita dele. Quanto mais “objetiva” a pauta, e mais “isento” o conteúdo, maior o poder nas mãos dos que controlam as redes.

 


Há que ter um ponto de vista, que nasce do próprio conhecimento dos jornalistas sobre a realidade, o contexto histórico e os personagens envolvidos, e que muitas vezes se perde na ânsia pela entrega da “mercadoria”. 


Mas, como observou

Fabiana Moraes

, parte da imprensa continua a repetir os erros cometidos na cobertura da Lava Jato, quando os jornalistas reproduziam as informações vazadas pela força-tarefa (havia até coletiva em off), selecionadas conforme os interesses dos envolvidos: o juiz Sérgio Moro (depois ministro da Justiça de Bolsonaro) e procuradores como Deltan Dallagnol, que quase conseguiu garfar 2,5 bilhões de reais de um acordo entre a Petrobrás e o Departamento de Justiça dos EUA para criar uma fundação privada. 


A Lava Jato só revelou seu real sentido para o país quando os jornalistas do Intercept Brasil demonstraram como esses interesses levaram a ilegalidades que comprometeram o processo. Fato que de certo modo se repetiu nessas eleições, quando o mesmo veículo expôs as relações de Flávio Bolsonaro com Daniel Vorcaro nos áudios do Dark Horse. Até então, o que se tinha eram os vazamentos seletivos de André Mendonça contra Alexandre de Moraes e “Lulinha”, motivados pelo desejo de eleger Flávio Bolsonaro – como se tornou explícito com a crise no STF e o 7 de setembro em São Paulo.


Houve outro erro, que também já foi apontado por Fabiana …

title: Agrivoltaico finanziato da Israele: alcuni aggiornamenti dalla Toscana e dal Piemonte
content:
Proponiamo di seguito un contributo che racconta il punto in cui i due percorsi territoriali, uno a Ribolla in provincia di Grosseto e uno in provincia di Biella e Vercelli, sono arrivati portando avanti la lotta contro l’agrivoltaico finanziato da Israele.


AGRIVOLTAICO ISRAELIANO IN TOSCANA: LA REGIONE HA IL POTERE DI FERMARLO, MA NON LO USA


Riceviamo e pubblichiamo da

Per Un’Altra Città


Di nuovo la Palestina ci dà la possibilità di conoscere il nostro sistema più a fondo, e di vederlo per quello che è. In questo caso è un abuso colto in flagrante, il progetto di un impianto agrivoltaico a Ribolla, a offrirci questa opportunità. Analizzeremo brevemente i fatti, e poi le reazioni di istituzioni e politici.

A Ribolla, provincia di Grosseto, un gruppo di cittadini 

ha scoperto

 che ad aver richiesto l’autorizzazione per la costruzione di un impianto agrivoltaico, sotto la dicitura di SPV Energy 3, si tratta di un colosso delle costruzioni israeliano, la Shikun e Binui. Questa non è semplicemente un’azienda israeliana, è una multinazionale complice di violazioni dei diritti umani commesse sul popolo palestinese. Ha costruito parte della barriera che cinge d’assedio Gaza, rendendola un campo di concentramento, ed ha realizzato impianti nei territori occupati illegalmente, facendo proprie e sfruttando terre e risorse non sue. Per questo è stata inserita nella banca dati dell’Alto Commissariato delle Nazioni Unite per i Diritti Umani che elenca le imprese coinvolte nell’occupazione illegale dei Territori Palestinesi Occupati. E per questo è stata oggetto di disinvestimenti da parte di importanti fondi sovrani e pensionistici internazionali (come il fondo pensione statale della Nuova Zelanda e quello della Norvegia), proprio per violazione delle linee guida etiche sui diritti umani.

I cittadini di Ribolla che hanno scoperto la reale proprietà dietro la SPV Energy 3 hanno così costituito un collettivo, Diritti in Palestina, ed iniziato una mobilitazione ed una raccolta firme, che in circa un mese ha raggiunto le 15000, ed ha ottenuto l’importante risultato di portare alla

luce l’esistenza di altri quattro progetti della Shikun e Binui sul territorio toscano, a diversi stadi di approvazione: Collesalvetti (località Mortaiolo), Grosseto (Località Podere Cavazza), Casciana Terme Lari (Pisa, Località Lavaiano) e Gavorrano (Grosseto, Località La Merlina). Grazie al loro lavoro quindi è stata svelato un fatto molto grave: un’azienda responsabile di crimini internazionali può investire, costruire, e fare profitti in Toscana attraverso società veicolo senza dipendenti e con poche migliaia di euro di capitale sociale, e nessuno nelle istituzioni se ne accorge.


È solo grazie al lavoro degli attivisti di Ribolla che le istituzioni sono state costrette ad esprimersi. La risposta di Giani, appena la questione è venuta fuori, 

è stata (9 agosto)

: “Al momento è tutto fermo perché stiamo lavorando a una legge sulle aree idonee per le rinnovabili, la nostra giunta ha presentato una proposta che verrà discussa a settembre, dopodiché valuteremo i singoli progetti”. La Regione ad agosto si impegnava a valutare “sulla base dell’aderenza o meno alla linea socio-economica e valoriale della Toscana espressa nella nostra proposta di legge”.

E Francesco Limatola (PD), sindaco di Roccastrada, comune di cui fa parte Ribolla, seppur con toni più in sintonia con la voce del territorio, ha tuttavia seguito la linea tracciata da Giani. 

Ha dichiarato

 che il progetto dev’essere fermato, proprio attraverso la nuova legge: “non possiamo

transigere. La transizione etica dev’essere anche eticamente responsabile. Uno strumento importante è la legge sulle aree idonee, se i nostri emendamenti verranno approvati dal Consiglio Regionale, potremo avere una transizione energetica che sia anche etica”.

Quindi sia Giani che Limatola fanno intendere, seppure senza dirlo esplicitamente, che con la nuova legge sulle aree idonee il progetto può essere fermato. Questo però si è rivelato essere falso, come ci hanno confermato direttamente due membri del Consiglio Regionale: questa legge non potrà essere applicata a progetti che sono stati già presentati. Inoltre nella legge non sono stati inseriti criteri etici, quindi non è certo con questa legge che potranno essere fermati progetti di aziende criminali, neppure in futuro.


Perché le due massime autorità sul territorio, Giani e Limatola, hanno offerto una soluzione inesistente? C’è davvero nelle …

author: Corey Larocque
title: Amagoalik controversy rooted in dissolution of health and social services boards
content:
Dennis Patterson


Recent news stories about a beloved Inuit elder John Amagoalik

seeking support

 from the Government of Nunavut to return and remain home in his autumn years drew me back to 1999: the first months of the promising new Nunavut government, in which we all had so much hope.


What happened in 1999 which may have led us to this situation?


Well, the first major law of the new Nunavut government proudly led by Nunavut’s first Inuk lawyer, then-premier Paul Okalik, was the Boards of Management Dissolution Act, which with one stroke, without consultation, dissolved all three existing regional health and social services boards in the brand new territory. (Disclosure: I was Chair of the Baffin board at the time this drastic decision was made — the only non-Inuk member of our 13-person board.)


Those boards were dominated by respected Inuit elders from every community in each of Nunavut’s three regions. We had been well trained in governance — the Carver Model — by the N.W.T. government and had done good work in four previous years under the Government of the Northwest Territories until being abruptly told we were no longer needed by the brand new Nunavut government.


In the Kitikmeot, the board had successfully pushed for a new regional health centre in Cambridge Bay that provided elder care to keep elderly residents in their homeland.


In the Kivalliq, the health board oversaw the first midwifery program to allow women to give birth closer to home, reviving traditional practices.


In the Qikiqtani Region, the health board made the bold decision to move southern medical services from Montreal to Ottawa, removing an additional language barrier for Inuit patients from Nunavut’s largest region. The board also chose the site and functional program which reflected Inuit values — for a new regional hospital, retaining and renovating the old hospital for administrative support.


Health boards run mostly by Inuit helped make those big decisions happen.


So in 1999, soon after the establishment of the shiny new Inuit-led Nunavut government, I remember Inuit board members being incredulous that their new government would do such a thing without even consulting them, instead relying on a quick and dirty desktop study by a now-defunct colonial federal agency — Consulting and Audit Canada — which justified that extreme action as a cost-saving measure, even though we all knew that the vast bulk of the budget was tied up in nurses’ salaries and medevac costs.


That reckless decision to dissolve the health boards also disrespected a condition of the transfers of health services from the federal to the territorial government in 1988. When Health was transferred to the GNWT  from the federal government, federal health minister Jake Epp made it a condition of the transfer that the territory had to agree to create health boards to ensure community input.


So when respected Inuit from communities in all three regions of Nunavut heard that their new government no longer required their advice, it was surprising and devastating.


I never understood why the new Nunavut government would deprive itself of the very valuable traditional knowledge of those respected (mostly) Inuit who served on those boards, representing each one of Nunavut’s communities in each region. Instead, the government promised to establish advisory local health committees in every community, which never materialized.


Our duties overseeing the operations and developing policies for health and social services in our regions were then taken over  by a well intentioned but utterly overwhelmed Nunavut minister of health and social services, originally from Newfoundland, who was married to an Inuk from Qikiqtani.


Even though he promised to be accessible, being the first one in his office at seven every morning, it was too much even for one workaholic and sincere minister to run those very important and culturally sensitive departments. He was overwhelmed by those huge responsibilities and ended his political career, exhausted,  after only two terms.


The negative impact of that inexplicable decision by the government of Paul Okalik is still felt  to this day and I believe is reflected in the current uncertain situation of John Amagoalik.


Would an Inuit-led health and social services board have ensured the provision of required homecare for a respected Inuit elder statesman?


If Inuit-led health boards had been allowed to continue instead of being …

author: Jon Queally
title: Fetterman Joins GOP to Block Iran War Powers Resolution — Again
content:
While four Republicans joined Democrats by voting in favor, Fetterman became the deciding vote.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania was the lone Democrat on Thursday to help Republicans in the US Senate vote down a resolution to end the “illegal” war of choice launched against Iran by President Donald Trump earlier this year.

In the 49-50 vote, the Republican majority blocked the latest resolution calling for an end to the war. While four Republicans — Susan Collins of Maine, Alaska’s Lisa Murkowski, Rand Paul of Kentucky and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — joined Democrats by voting in favor, Fetterman became the deciding vote.

Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.) was among those expressing frustration with Fetterman, a lawmaker who has become a thorn in the side of his party since taking office and taking a hard right with his pro-war positions, accommodations to Trump, and determined support for pro-Israeli policies.

“John Fetterman just cast the deciding vote to keep the Iran War raging,” said Deluzio. “This reckless war has cost American lives, innocent lives, tens of billions of dollars, and higher prices on nearly everything here at home. John and 49 Republican Senators voted in favor of all of that.”

“Fetterman never fails to disappoint,” said Susan Wild, a former Democratic member of the US House from Pennsylvania.

The vote came on the same day that an advocacy group representing American citizens with Iranian heritage sued the Trump administration for usurping the powers of Congress when it launched an “unconstitutional” war against Iran — a military conflict that has lasted nearly 7 months with no end in sight, causing misery across the Middle East and economic pain worldwide, including in the United States.

Filed in the US District Court for the District of Columbia on Thursday, the lawsuit, filed on behalf of the National Iranian American Council Action (NIAC Action), asks the court to declare that President Donald Trump’s unprovoked attack on Iran violates the Constitution’s Declare War Clause.

In a statement, NIAC Action said the suit was brought “on behalf of its members whose families have been injured, displaced, economically devastated and are in continuing mortal danger as a result of a war that was never lawfully authorized.”

Launched on Feb. 28, the US attack, in coordination with the Israeli government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, was launched despite ongoing diplomatic efforts and active talks over US sanctions against Iran and questions about Iran’s domestic nuclear program and its conventional missile capabilities. The war was initiated, according to the group,

without a declaration of war or other congressional authorization and that the war has continued, including repeated heavy bombardments and a naval blockade, despite this lack of authorization and the passage by both chambers of Congress of an explicit directive to terminate unauthorized hostilities against Iran.

“No President should have the power to take this country into an indefinite war by himself,” said NIAC Action president Jamal Abdi, in a statement. “Congress never authorized this war. Yet Iranian families are being bombed, American service members have been killed, and communities on both sides are being forced to bear the consequences. This lawsuit asks a fundamental question: can one person decide, on his own, to keep an entire nation at war?”

NIAC Action offered the example of one plaintiff, Nima Dilmaghani, whose cousin in Iran was injured when the company warehouse where she worked was bombed. Dilmaghani’s cousin, the group explained, “suffered a broken leg, serious damage to their eardrums, and the loss of their index finger, which surgeons reattached but which has lost motion. Approximately ten of her coworkers were killed, and approximately ten more were injured. In a separate bombing, their apartment was destroyed while they were away at work. They are now working two jobs to survive.” Other NIAC Action members have detailed similar stories.

Lawyers behind the lawsuit said that just because President Trump and other officials, including Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, have tried to argue that war against Iran is not a “war,” that does not make it so.

author: Unknown
title: Barınç: Martyr Dîlan’s heart belonged to her struggle and her land
content:
The Coordination of the Kurdistan Women’s Liberation Party (PAJK) announced recently that Dîlan Şirnex (Rabia Barınç) joined the caravan of martyrs on 17 September 2026 after suffering from cancer.


Her brother Selim and her friends Rahime Arzu and Leyla Arzu İlhan spoke to ANF about martyr Dîlan’s life, her struggle and her devotion to her people and her land.


Selim Barınç said they grew up in a patriotic family from Şırnak (Şirnex) and described his sister, martyr Dîlan, in the following words: “We were four brothers and four sisters, and comrade Dîlan was the eldest of us. She truly was a very determined person, from her childhood until her martyrdom. Once she said something, no one could make her change her mind. Comrade Dîlan had tremendous willpower and conviction. She loved her land, she loved Abdullah Öcalan, and she loved her struggle. I believe that we and her comrades will certainly carry her goals through to success.


Comrade Dîlan was the eldest of us. I used to say that if we ever lost our mother and father, comrade Dîlan would be both a mother and a father to us. But comrade Dîlan attained martyrdom.


Wherever comrade Dîlan went, she always left a mark with her natural manner, simplicity, humility and sense of humour. She was also very compassionate. She was a strong-willed and loving person. As long as we are alive, comrade Dîlan will continue to live in our hearts.”


Rahime Arzu, the wife of a martyr who had known Dîlan for 20 years, said: “Whenever comrade Dîlan came to our home, she would tell me, ‘You are my sister.’ I have three children, and she would tell them, ‘Call me aunt so that I can be your mother’s sister.’


She called me about a month ago and said, ‘Bring the children. I want to see you and them.’ I went to see her in Sulaymaniyah (Silêmanî) and visited her at the hospital.


As comrade Selim said, she had a great sense of humour. Despite her pain and illness, she was still joking and making the children laugh. Her love for children was something else entirely. She never cared whose child they were and never made any distinction between them. Wherever she went, people inevitably grew fond of her, and she made them feel as though she were part of their family. She formed strong bonds with people. That is why it was not only our family. There are hundreds of families in the camp, for example, and many wanted to attend comrade Dîlan’s funeral. But the enemy had placed the entire area under blockade, and even those who came had to make their way there secretly. As long as my three daughters and I are alive, we will not allow comrade Dîlan to be forgotten. As long as we breathe, we will follow in the footsteps of our martyrs and never turn away from their path. Once again, we say, ‘Şehîd Namirin’ (Martyrs never die).”


Either I will be martyred in Kobanê or I will see Kobanê liberated


Leyla Arzu İlhan, whose father and two siblings were martyred in the Kurdistan Freedom Struggle, began by commemorating the martyrs of Kurdistan’s freedom struggle in the person of martyr Dîlan.


Leyla Arzu İlhan said, “Every martyr is a memory for us; every martyr gives us strength to struggle; every martyr gives us the will to intensify the struggle,” and adding that she had known martyr Dîlan Şirnex since childhood.


 


 Leyla Arzu İlhan described martyr Dîlan in the following words: “Comrade Dîlan and I were childhood friends. Our friendship continued from the 1990s until today. Wherever we were, we would always find a way to reach each other. Comrade Dîlan was truly someone who remained committed to every decision she made until the very end. She was fully committed to her decision to struggle. Without hesitation, without doubt and without tiring, she was constantly engaged in struggle, no matter what field she was in. In the struggle, she was always a source of morale for her comrades and always strengthened their struggle. She could spend days helping her comrades and would never say she was tired. She put tremendous effort into everything. Sometimes, when we told her, ‘You are tired, don’t do it,’ she would say, ‘Even if I am tired, I will continue to work for my comrades.’ She was committed to her comrades, to life and to the struggle until the very end.


Even during her illness, I believe that until the moment she was martyred, she never once thought that her life would end this way. Many times when we spoke to her or visited her, we would say, ‘Let’s not do this, it isn’t good for you …

title: Iraq's Najaf Airport suspends flights to Iran
content:
The management of Najaf International Airport announced in a statement that all flights to Iran have been suspended in accordance with official directives.


According to the statement, all flights between Iran and Najaf International Airport are suspended indefinitely as of 2:00 p.m. today, based on official instructions.


The airport management informed all airlines and relevant parties of the decision to halt flights and requested compliance with the directives.


Iran’s leading airlines were forced to cancel their international flights on Wednesday after Washington announced that it would make no concessions to companies supporting them.


If they fail to comply with the U.S. sanctions, those companies will also face the risk of being blacklisted and consequently excluded from the dollar-denominated financial system.


The same happened on September 8 to companies in Turkey, Malaysia, the United Arab Emirates, and Kazakhstan that had cooperated with Mahan Air.


U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Wednesday, “We are putting the Iranians under unprecedented pressure.”


According to Bessent, “More than 80 to 90 percent of international flights departing from Iran have been suspended.”


Speaking on Fox News, the secretary made a sarcastic remark, saying, “I’m not quite sure how the Iranian representatives at the UN are going to get back to their country.”

author: Unknown
title: Tons of felled trees transported out of Besta by trucks
content:
New footage has emerged of the logging that has been continuing for years in the Besta region in the countryside of Şırnak province. The footage published by the Mezopotamya Agency shows trees reportedly cut down in February and left in the area to dry being loaded onto trucks and transported out of the region.


The footage shows how the trees are loaded by village guards brought from Hosyan village in Şırnak’s Pervari district and transported through military checkpoints. The trucks, which are covered with tarpaulins, reportedly have Ankara license plates beginning with 06, while tons of additional timber are said to remain in the area awaiting transport.


Logging has continued for nearly seven years in central Şırnak and its districts, as well as in the Cudi and Gabar mountains and the Besta region, causing serious ecological destruction in the area.


There is no definitive information about where the felled trees are being taken. According to local sources, some of the timber is being transported to surrounding cities for use as fuel in bread ovens or taken to other areas to be used as firewood during the winter.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Ungava advance polls to open Saturday
content:
Advance polls for the Ungava riding in Quebec’s provincial election open Saturday, and staff from the provincial elections authority will be in each Nunavik community to help make voting more accessible.


Élections Québec spokesperson Julie St-Arnaud-Drolet said visiting remote communities ahead of the Oct. 5 election day is part of an effort to address the historically low voter turn out in Nunavik. It’s also a priority because they often struggle to contact electors through traditional means like the mail, she said.


“Last election, electors in Inuit communities didn’t receive their reminder cards, for example,” St-Arnaud-Drolet said about the 2022 election, in which they weren’t able to reach some residents because they didn’t have access to their post office box addresses.


In that same election, only 30 per cent of eligible Ungava voters — who live in the province’s largest riding by geography, at more than 855,000 square kilometres — showed up.


This year, from Sept. 26 to 30 — the advance polling dates in Nunavik —  Élections Québec staff will help residents get on the elector list to participate in the election, in which five candidates

are running

 in Ungava.


Voters will be able to cast their ballot from their village’s municipal office, except for those in Kuujjuaraapik, who must go to the community’s cultural centre.


Élections Québec targeted post office boxes across Inuit, Cree and Naskapi communities with information sheets detailing how to vote in English, French and in each community’s local language — a first for the agency, St-Arnaud-Drolet said.


She said staff also want to recruit locals to run the election in each of Nunavik’s 14 communities.


“If there’s local people interested in working during the day of the election, it would be fantastic, because they would be able to offer service in Inuktitut,” she said, adding that, while they’ve had some success recruiting Cree staff, they’ve struggled to attract Inuit.


She said Inuktitut will be also be displayed at voting polls but noted the ballots displaying candidate names will be in French only because the election agency wanted the full, proper names of each political party to be displayed.


The decision to offer French-only ballots on election day has generated criticism from the Avataq Cultural Institute, an Inuit cultural organization which defends the preservation of the Inuktitut language.


While its president, William Tagoona, was relieved to find information about the election in Inuktitut earlier this week in his mailbox, he said the translation should extend to the ballots as well.


“Who wants to mark a ballot that they don’t understand?” he said in an interview.


Many Inuit across Nunavik don’t speak French, with census data from 2021 showing 8,770 out of 13,985 Indigenous respondents, or 62 per cent, reported speaking English only. A total of 1,550 respondents, or 11 per cent, reported speaking neither French or English.


Tagoona was also disappointed that Quebec’s language law had initially forced Élections Québec to mail out voting materials in French only. As far back as 2023, the agency has asked to be exempt from the language law, which, since 2022, has forced government institutions to issue public communications only in French.


That changed on Sept. 16, after a Quebec Superior Court judge issued an emergency order asking Élections Québec to distribute information about the election in English too, following outcry from Montreal’s anglophone community.


Quebec’s ministry responsible for the protection of the French language declined to respond to Tagoona’s critiques, citing the civil suit before the Quebec Superior Court.

title: The Hague Group: South Africa Leads Coalition Against U.S./Israel's "Unilateral Bullying" of the ICC
content:
At the United Nations this week, President Trump repeated his attacks on the International Criminal Court and urged other nations to pull out of the global tribunal. The United States earlier this year imposed sanctions on the president of the

ICC

 and a senior prosecutor who was part of the team that issued an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for crimes against humanity in Gaza, and the Trump administration is reportedly preparing more sanctions against the institution itself. Meanwhile, a coalition of nations has formed to defend international law in solidarity with the people of Palestine under the banner of the Hague Group, which was established last year by Bolivia, Colombia, Cuba, Honduras, Malaysia, Namibia, Senegal and South Africa.


“It’s an absolute low point for the sacred grounds of the United Nations that President Trump has shown up here and attacked the international legal order,” says Varsha Gandikota, executive secretary of the Hague Group.


We also air remarks from South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola, who spoke earlier this week at the historic Riverside Church in New York City to urge respect for international law.

title: SÜDEF President Türker: We support the peace process
content:
Evgil Türker, President of the Federation of Syriac Associations (SÜDEF), spoke to ANF about the Peace and Democratic Society Process.


Türker said the process, which gained momentum with the Call for Peace and Democratic Society, offers hope for minorities and particularly for Syriacs. He said the vast majority of Syriacs were forced to migrate because of intense conflict, unresolved killings and various state policies targeting those it did not consider its own, recalling that the more peaceful environment created during previous processes enabled Syriacs to return to Turkey.


Türker said, “Sayfo has now become an identity for Syriacs,” and stressing that although the Syriac community withdrew into itself because of the traumas it experienced and has largely remained distant from politics, it is following the process and has serious expectations.


What does this process, which aims to move the historical Kurdish-Turkish relationship from a ground of war and conflict to one of democratic society and peace, mean for other minorities in the country?


The process of moving away from war and conflict towards democratic society and peace means many things for minorities, particularly Syriacs. As is well known, Syriacs were forced to migrate because of the conflict in the region in the mid-1980s and particularly in the early 1990s.


At the time, there were between 50 and 60 unresolved killings of Syriacs. People were killed in various Syriac villages. Murders whose perpetrators were known but which were nevertheless described as unresolved were committed in Midyat city centre, İdil (Hezex), Silopi, Beytüşşebap and Şırnak (Şirnex). At the time, Hizbulkontra groups were extensively used as hitmen. There was a wave of unresolved killings targeting Christian, Syriac, Armenian and Yazidi minorities here, as well as Kurdish patriots.


Syriacs who migrated returned to Turkey after Mr. Öcalan’s call


Syriacs were forced to migrate during that period. They could not even visit these places as they can today, not until 2005. In 1999, following a call by Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) leader Abdullah Öcalan, the Kurdish Movement’s guerrillas withdrew from Turkey. The end of the fighting created a more secure environment for people. Syriacs began travelling back and forth to their own country and their own lands. As peace processes developed, Syriacs also began returning to Turkey. We experienced the same thing during the 2013–2015 resolution process.


How does the Syriac community view the process?


Syriacs living here generally remain somewhat distant from politics. The conflict of the previous period inevitably caused the Syriac community to withdraw into itself. Apart from some exceptions, the community stays away from politics. But from the discussions we hold in Mardin, in urban centres and in villages, we can see that the Syriac community is following this process and is very hopeful. They know that as the process develops, it will open up greater space for many things, including freedom of thought and expression and democratic action.


The Call for Peace and Democratic Society was truly of vital importance for Syriacs as well. Syriacs are following the process, and we as institutions are aware of this. People ask us about it; rather than relying on the press, they approach us and our institutions directly. Following the Call for Peace and Democratic Society, we held a well-attended public meeting with officials from the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) at our federation headquarters in June 2025. We discussed what this call meant for minorities and Syriacs. Many questions came from Syriacs.


Syriacs want to return to their country and their villages and protect their land and values. They have serious expectations. We believe that as this process develops in a healthy way, our people will return to their own lands. Of course, there is still some anxiety among the people: “Will it really happen or not?” Despite these concerns, however, we see that compared with previous attempts, this process is on firmer ground and is being pursued more seriously and cautiously.


Lasting peace is difficult without a commission and confronting past wrongs


The Kurdish Movement is calling for Truth Investigation Commissions to be established. As we mark 111 years since the Sayfo Syriac Genocide of 15 June, do you think lasting peace is possible without confronting the past?

title: Kaya family gets their daughter’s remains after 27 years
content:
The identities of Süheyla Kaya and Zehra Kısaoğlu, whose remains were among those exhumed from Garzan Cemetery in the countryside of Tatvan, Bitlis, in 2017 and taken to Kilyos Cemetery in Istanbul, were established through DNA testing.


Following years of applications and DNA procedures, the families of Süheyla Kaya and Zehra Kısaoğlu confirmed the identities of their daughters through a DNA match conducted at the Council of Forensic Medicine on September 21. The families took the remains they received from Kilyos Cemetery back to their hometowns.


Süheyla Kaya was buried in Karlıova, while Zehra Kısaoğlu was buried in Bingöl in ceremonies held for each. Following the burials, condolence gatherings were held in the villages of Kargapazarı and Çira Cor, where the families live.


27 years looking for their daughter's remains


Süheyla Kaya’s mother, Fakite Kaya, described the years-long struggle to find her daughter’s remains. Speaking to Mezopotamya Agency (MA), Fakite Kaya said that after learning of allegations concerning a mass grave in Garzan, they applied to the relevant authorities and provided DNA samples. She said they were informed years later that her daughter’s remains had been found.


“Our hearts are deeply broken, and all those mothers’ hearts are broken too. Having to go through so much hardship just to find even the bones of a child is extremely painful,” Fakite Kaya said, wishing patience to the other families searching for the remains of their children. Fakite Kaya added: “May they all be reunited with a part of their children.”


Süheyla Kaya’s father, Selahattin Kaya, said that he had waited for news of his daughter for 27 years and expressed his hope that families who have not yet recovered the remains of their loved ones will also be reunited with them at the end of the same process.


Selahattin Kaya said: “May there also be a hopeful process for those who have not been able to find their children’s remains, and may they find them.” The family expressed their hope that the ongoing process would conclude successfully and that a “free and dignified peace” would be achieved.

title: Conference in London will address Kurdish question and peace processes
content:
London will host a conference focusing on a democratic and political solution to the Kurdish question and international peace processes.


Organized by the Centre for Kurdish Affairs at Hamilton House on September 29–30, the “Peace and Democratic Integration Conference” will bring together Kurdish politicians, academics, journalists, civil society representatives, and experts who have been involved in peace processes in different countries.


Former British Foreign Secretary and Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy, along with Labour MPs Catherine West and Bambos Charalambous, have expressed their support for the aims of the conference, which the organizers said are: "To establish London as a strategic forum for inclusive and informed dialogue on peace, democratic transition, and the Kurdish question; to draw on the United Kingdom’s experience of managing political conflict, competing national claims, and constitutional change through democratic consent, negotiation, devolution, and power-sharing; To ensure that political, regional, cultural, and gender diversity is meaningfully represented throughout the process; To translate comparative learning into credible, practical, and forward-looking policy options.


Peace experiences from around the world to be discussed


On the first day of the conference, peace processes in the North of Ireland, Colombia, South Africa, the Basque Country, Catalonia, and South Tyrol will be examined.


Issues including negotiation and political dialogue, the transition from armed conflict to democratic politics, disarmament, reintegration, power-sharing, autonomy, and constitutional guarantees will be discussed through the experiences of different countries.


Victoria Sandino, who was involved in Colombia’s peace process, will also participate in the conference via a video message.


Second day to focus on the Kurdish question


Sessions on September 30 will focus directly on the political, legal, social, and regional dimensions of the Kurdish question.


The future of Kurdish politics, democratic representation, local government, and the role of civil society and the diaspora will be discussed, while the impact of developments in Turkey, Syria, Iraq, and Iran on Kurds will also be assessed.


The programme will also cover the role of women in peace processes, minority participation, human rights, freedom of the press, and social reconciliation.


Speakers at the conference will include figures from Kurdish politics such as Pervin Buldan, Gültan Kışanak, Gülüstan Kılıç Koçyiğit, Serpil Kemalbay, and Osman Baydemir, as well as academics, journalists, and experts working on international peace processes.


How can lasting peace be built?


Nejla Ari, Coordinator of the Centre for Kurdish Affairs, said the conference aims to bring together peace experiences from different countries and the political experiences of Kurds on the same platform. Ari said that ending armed conflict, maintaining political dialogue, and establishing legal frameworks for disarmament and reintegration are important areas to address in achieving a lasting solution.


One of the conference’s central questions will be: “How can the process of moving away from armed conflict be transformed into a lasting, democratic, and inclusive political solution?”


The organizers have also identified the meaningful participation of women, minorities, civil society, and communities affected by conflict in peace processes as one of the conference’s central areas of discussion.

title: He walked, and a people followed in his footsteps
content:
It all began in Tuzluçayır, a shantytown in Ankara. It was a stronghold of leftist organizations. In those years, the police could not enter the neighborhood. It was therefore known as “Little Moscow.”


After Comrade Rıza met Kemal Pir, the Apoists began coming and going. The Altun family’s house was no longer large enough to accommodate everyone who came. The Apoists demolished the house with their own hands and rebuilt it as a larger home. Before long, this house became the Apoists’ headquarters in Ankara. Who didn’t pass through its doors? From Abdullah Öcalan to Kemal Pir, from Sakine Cansız to Ali Haydar Kaytan, it was a regular gathering place for all the cadres of the early period. It served as a center for education and accommodation.


As Tuzluçayır became the headquarters of the Apoists, the neighborhood’s young people also began joining them, following Comrade Rıza and the first group. With the participation of Tuzluçayır’s youth, followed by the support of their families, the Apoist group grew considerably. Comrade Rıza would later joke about those days:


“We didn’t join the Apoists; the Apoists joined us. Our group was much bigger than theirs.”


Indeed, a march was held in Ankara in the mid-1970s. For the first time, the Apoists took part in a demonstration under their own banners. Comrade Rıza and his friends gathered everyone they could from the neighborhood—old and young, women and children—and brought them to the march. The Apoists had the largest turnout at that demonstration.


Comrade Rıza was the leading figure and leader of the group made up of young people from Tuzluçayır. Because of his ability to rally young people around him, his quick thinking, and his organizational skills, he was nicknamed “Şirket” (“The Company”). In those years, everyone in Tuzluçayır, from the left to the right, knew Comrade Rıza as “Şirket.”


As they expanded their organization, the Apoists also began engaging in clashes with the police and right-wing groups, while becoming increasingly visible in marches and similar actions. This drew all eyes in Ankara toward the Apoists.


Mother Hatice bought him the first gun


At the time, Comrade Rıza and his friends knew the neighborhood so well that they would lure the police into chasing them, running from one street to another and keeping them on their heels.


Because the Şirket family home had become a center for the Apoists, it was targeted by the Turkish state. Raids on the house, along with the detention, arrest, and torture of members of the Altun family, became routine.


By then, the family had also developed a strong awareness of the enemy. No one asked the names of those who came and went, and nothing about what was discussed in the house or about its visitors was mentioned to anyone in the neighborhood or at school. During police raids, the children would even pretend to be asleep so that they would not be questioned. If an organizational document or book had been hidden somewhere in the house, they would deliberately look in other directions so the police would not notice.


In fact, it was Mother Hatice who bought him his first gun.


Once the Apoist Movement had achieved a certain level of organization, it turned its attention toward Kurdistan. Comrade Rıza was among those who went to Kurdistan in late 1976. He carried out activities in Urfa and Antep for a long period.


The Siverek-Hilvan area became the focal point of the Apoists’ struggle in Kurdistan against collaboration, betrayal, and all forms of reactionism. Comrade Rıza remained there and continued the struggle until his capture. While organizing the people on the one hand, he also took part in a major struggle against the Turkish state through confronting collaboration on the other.


A history was written


By then, Comrade Rıza had become a well-known figure in the Siverek-Hilvan area, recognized by friend and foe alike. Yet no one in Siverek or Hilvan knew him by his real name. Neither the name Rıza nor the nickname Şirket meant anything to them. He had become the “Kıvırcık Ali” of Siverek and Hilvan. Ask anyone, and they knew him as “Kıvırcık Ali.”


In 1982, our path took us to Siverek. We were taken from house to house, street to street. In front of every house and at every coffeehouse, people told us about the resistance of Kıvırcık Ali and his comrades. A history had been written there…

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Susan Aglukark seeks new distributor for upcoming music release
content:
Susan Aglukark is looking for a new distributing partner for her latest project, which has pushed back the release of the lead single from her upcoming EP

Disco Ball

.


The song,

F

or You

, was originally scheduled to release Sept. 8.


The company that previously distributed Aglukark’s music, the Independent Digital Licensing Agency, was sold in 2023 to Round Hill Music, a subsidiary of a U.S. private equity firm. The agency’s former manager retired within the past year.


Aglukark said since then, she has been looking for a company that will help her publish her new music on online streaming platforms, like Spotify.


“The streaming side is a completely different beast because it’s a learning curve and requires time to watch the numbers, such as the number of downloads,” said Aglukark. “It made sense for us to find a partner to handle that side of things.”


As an independent artist, Aglukark and her husband, sound engineer and recording partner Jacques Poirier, have been managing the business side of her music career since 1993, through her independent record label and management company, Aglukark Entertainment.


She said that she manages all inquiries for concerts and keynote speeches, as well as her own recording time in the studio.


“I

t really is a challenge for us right now to find the right home for our music,” Aglukark said.


For You

began as a poem titled

Igvit

 she wrote in 2022, inspired by Indigenous communities confronting the loss of children who never returned home from residential schools.


Aglukark invited singer Sweleyén, also known as Julianne Peters, of the Tsq’éscen’ First Nation in British Columbia, to translate a verse into Secwepemctsín. 


Peters is from near Kamloops, where the Tk’emlúps te Secwépemc First Nation announced in May 2021 that ground-penetrating radar had identified what it described as 215 potential unmarked graves at the former Kamloops Indian Residential School.


“It just turned into this really beautiful collaboration,” Aglukark said.


Aglukark later decided the song should be told through the voices of young people and asked choir director Mary Piercey-Lewis to help bring a youth choir into the project.


The choir recorded in Toronto, as well as in Iqaluit in March, with about 10 to 15 singers.

The song also brought together singer and composer Deantha Edmunds and the Inuksuk Drum Dancers from Iqaluit.


The project received support from the Ontario Arts Council. Proceeds from

 For You

 will go to the Orange Shirt Society and Aglukark’s Arctic Rose Foundation, which supports Indigenous youth through the arts.


Aglukark said she is talks with a few distributing partners and hopes to release the song soon, with the five-song EP

Disco Ball

 planned for early 2027.
